Let \(p=503\). Note that \(502=p-1\).

### 1) Roots-of-unity / character filter in \(\mathbb F_p\)
For \(r\in\{0,1,\dots,501\}\), define
\[
S_r=\sum_{m\ge 0}\binom{10000}{502m+r}.
\]
In \(\mathbb F_p^\*\), every element \(a\neq 0\) satisfies \(a^{502}=1\). Consider
\[
A_r:=\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{-r}(1+a)^{10000}\in\mathbb F_p.
\]
Expand \((1+a)^{10000}=\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}a^k\):
\[
A_r=\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{k-r}.
\]
But
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{t}=
\begin{cases}
502 & \text{if }502\mid t,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence only terms with \(k\equiv r\pmod{502}\) survive, giving
\[
A_r=502\,S_r \quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
\]
Since \(502\equiv -1\pmod{503}\), it is invertible mod \(503\), so
\[
S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\iff A_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}.
\]

### 2) Reduce \((1+a)^{10000}\) modulo \(p\)
For \(a\neq -1\), \(1+a\in\mathbb F_p^\*\) so \((1+a)^{502}=1\). Thus
\[
(1+a)^{10000}=(1+a)^{10000\bmod 502}=(1+a)^{462}\quad (a\neq -1),
\]
and for \(a=-1\), \((1+a)^{10000}=0\). Therefore
\[
A_r=\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*,\,a\neq -1} a^{-r}(1+a)^{462}.
\]

Let \(b=1+a\). Then \(a=b-1\), and \(a\neq 0,-1\) corresponds to \(b\neq 1,0\). We get
\[
A_r=\sum_{b\in\mathbb F_p\setminus\{0,1\}} (b-1)^{-r}b^{462}.
\]
Since \(b\neq 1\), \((b-1)^{-r}=(b-1)^{502-r}\). Let \(s=502-r\) (so \(s\in\{1,2,\dots,502\}\), with \(s=502\) when \(r=0\)). Then
\[
A_r=\sum_{b\in\mathbb F_p\setminus\{0,1\}} b^{462}(b-1)^s.
\]
The terms at \(b=0\) and \(b=1\) are \(0\) (since \(462>0\) and \(s>0\)), so we may sum over all \(b\in\mathbb F_p\):
\[
A_r=\sum_{b\in\mathbb F_p} b^{462}(b-1)^s.
\]

### 3) Expand and use power sums over \(\mathbb F_p\)
Expand:
\[
b^{462}(b-1)^s=\sum_{j=0}^s \binom{s}{j}(-1)^{s-j} b^{462+j}.
\]
So
\[
A_r=\sum_{j=0}^s \binom{s}{j}(-1)^{s-j}\sum_{b\in\mathbb F_p} b^{462+j}.
\]
In \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
\sum_{b\in\mathbb F_p} b^t=
\begin{cases}
-1 & \text{if }t\equiv 0\pmod{502}\text{ and }t>0,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Now \(462+j\) ranges from \(462\) to \(462+s\le 964\). The only positive multiple of \(502\) in this range is \(502\), occurring exactly when \(462+j=502\), i.e. \(j=40\).

- If \(s<40\) (equivalently \(r>462\)), then no such \(j\) occurs, hence \(A_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\), so \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\).
- If \(s\ge 40\) (equivalently \(r\le 462\)), then the only contributing term is \(j=40\), giving
  \[
  A_r\equiv \binom{s}{40}(-1)^{s-40}\cdot(-1)=(-1)^{s-39}\binom{s}{40}\pmod{503}.
  \]
  Here \(s\le 502<503\), so \(\binom{s}{40}\) is a nonzero integer and cannot be divisible by \(503\). Thus \(A_r\not\equiv 0\), so \(S_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{503}\).

Therefore, exactly those \(r\) with \(r=463,464,\dots,501\) give \(S_r\) divisible by \(503\).

Count:
\[
501-463+1=39.
\]

\[
\boxed{39}
\]

Let \(p=503\). We work modulo \(p\).

### 1) Roots-of-unity filter in \(\mathbb F_{503}\)
Since \(502=p-1\), the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_{503}^\times\) has order \(502\), so it contains a primitive \(502\)-nd root of unity \(\omega\).

Define
\[
A_r=\frac1{502}\sum_{j=0}^{501}\omega^{-rj}(1+\omega^j)^{10000}\in\mathbb F_{503}.
\]
Expand \((1+\omega^j)^{10000}=\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}\omega^{jk}\). Then
\[
A_r=\frac1{502}\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}\sum_{j=0}^{501}\omega^{j(k-r)}.
\]
The inner sum equals \(502\) if \(k\equiv r\pmod{502}\), and \(0\) otherwise. Hence in \(\mathbb F_{503}\),
\[
A_r=\sum_{m\ge0}\binom{10000}{502m+r}=S_r.
\]
So we may compute \(S_r \pmod{503}\) by evaluating \(A_r\).

### 2) Rewrite as a sum over \(\mathbb F_{503}^\times\)
As \(j\) runs \(0,\dots,501\), \(\omega^j\) runs over all \(a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times\). Thus
\[
S_r=\frac1{502}\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^{-r}(1+a)^{10000}.
\]
For \(a\neq -1\), we have \((1+a)^{502}=1\), so
\[
(1+a)^{10000}=(1+a)^{10000\bmod 502}=(1+a)^{462}.
\]
For \(a=-1\), the term is \(0^{10000}=0\), so the same formula holds. Therefore
\[
S_r=\frac1{502}\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^{-r}(1+a)^{462}.
\]
Since \(502\equiv -1\pmod{503}\), we have \(\frac1{502}\equiv -1\pmod{503}\), hence
\[
S_r\equiv -\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^{-r}(1+a)^{462}\pmod{503}.
\]
Write \(a^{-r}=a^{502-r}\) in \(\mathbb F_{503}^\times\). Let \(k=502-r\) (so \(k\in\{1,2,\dots,502\}\)). Then
\[
S_r\equiv -\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^{k}(1+a)^{462}\pmod{503}.
\]

### 3) Expand and use \(\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\times}a^m\)
Expand \((1+a)^{462}=\sum_{t=0}^{462}\binom{462}{t}a^t\). Then
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^k(1+a)^{462}
=\sum_{t=0}^{462}\binom{462}{t}\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^{k+t}.
\]
We use:
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^m=
\begin{cases}
502,& 502\mid m,\\
0,& 502\nmid m.
\end{cases}
\]
Here \(1\le k\le 502\) and \(0\le t\le 462\), so \(k+t\) ranges from \(1\) to \(964\). The only multiple of \(502\) in that range is \(502\). Thus the sum is nonzero exactly when
\[
k+t=502 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t=502-k.
\]
This requires \(0\le 502-k\le 462\), i.e. \(40\le k\le 502\). Therefore:
- If \(k\le 39\), the whole sum is \(0\), so \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\).
- If \(40\le k\le 502\), then
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times} a^k(1+a)^{462}
=502\binom{462}{502-k}\equiv -\binom{462}{502-k}\pmod{503},
\]
so
\[
S_r\equiv -\left(-\binom{462}{502-k}\right)=\binom{462}{502-k}\pmod{503}.
\]
But \(502-k=502-(502-r)=r\), hence for \(r\le 462\),
\[
S_r\equiv \binom{462}{r}\pmod{503}.
\]

### 4) Determine when \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\)
- For \(r=463,464,\dots,501\): we have \(k=502-r\le 39\), so \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\). That gives \(501-463+1=39\) values.
- For \(0\le r\le 462\): \(S_r\equiv \binom{462}{r}\pmod{503}\). Since \(503>462\), none of the integers \(\binom{462}{r}\) are divisible by \(503\) (their prime factors are \(\le 462\)). So no additional \(r\) work.

Hence exactly \(39\) of the \(S_r\) are multiples of \(503\).

\[
\boxed{39}
\]

Let \(p=503\). Note that \(502=p-1\), so the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^\*\) has order \(502\).

---

### 1) Roots-of-unity filter for \(S_r\)
Let \(\omega\) be a primitive \(502\)-nd root of unity. Then the standard filter gives
\[
S_r=\sum_{m\ge 0}\binom{10000}{502m+r}
=\frac1{502}\sum_{j=0}^{501}\omega^{-rj}(1+\omega^j)^{10000}.
\]
Reducing this congruence modulo \(p\), we may interpret \(\omega^j\) as running through all elements of \(\mathbb F_p^\*\). Thus
\[
S_r \equiv \frac1{502}\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{-r}(1+a)^{10000}\pmod p.
\]
Since \(502\equiv -1\pmod p\), we have \(\frac1{502}\equiv -1\pmod p\), so
\[
S_r \equiv -\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{-r}(1+a)^{10000}\pmod p.
\]
Therefore \(p\mid S_r\) iff
\[
T_r:=\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{-r}(1+a)^{10000}\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]

---

### 2) Reduce the exponent \(10000\) modulo \(502\)
For \(a\neq -1\), we have \(1+a\in\mathbb F_p^\*\), hence \((1+a)^{502}=1\). So
\[
(1+a)^{10000}=(1+a)^{10000\bmod 502}.
\]
Compute \(10000=502\cdot 19+462\), so \(10000\bmod 502=462\). Also, when \(a=-1\), \((1+a)^{10000}=0\) anyway. Hence
\[
T_r=\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{-r}(1+a)^{462}.
\]

---

### 3) Expand and use \(\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^t\)
Expand:
\[
(1+a)^{462}=\sum_{k=0}^{462}\binom{462}{k}a^k.
\]
Then
\[
T_r=\sum_{k=0}^{462}\binom{462}{k}\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{k-r}.
\]
In \(\mathbb F_p^\*\) (a cyclic group of order \(502\)),
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\*} a^{t}=
\begin{cases}
502,& 502\mid t,\\
0,& 502\nmid t.
\end{cases}
\]
Now \(k\in[0,462]\) and \(r\in[0,501]\). Since \(462<502\), the congruence \(k\equiv r\pmod{502}\) can only happen when \(r=k\) (and only if \(r\le 462\)).

- If \(r\ge 463\), then there is **no** \(k\in[0,462]\) with \(k\equiv r\pmod{502}\), so every inner sum is \(0\), hence
  \[
  T_r=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad p\mid S_r.
  \]

- If \(0\le r\le 462\), only the term \(k=r\) survives:
  \[
  T_r=502\binom{462}{r}\equiv -\binom{462}{r}\pmod p,
  \]
  so
  \[
  S_r\equiv -T_r \equiv \binom{462}{r}\pmod p.
  \]
  Since \(p=503>462\), none of the factorials in \(\binom{462}{r}=\frac{462!}{r!(462-r)!}\) is divisible by \(503\), so \(\binom{462}{r}\not\equiv 0\pmod{503}\). Thus \(p\nmid S_r\) for \(0\le r\le 462\).

---

### 4) Count the multiples
Exactly those \(r\in\{463,464,\dots,501\}\) give \(503\mid S_r\). The count is
\[
501-463+1=39.
\]

\[
\boxed{39}
\]

Let
\[
(1+x)^{10000}=\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}x^k.
\]
Reducing this polynomial modulo \(x^{502}-1\) identifies \(x^{502}\equiv 1\), so all terms with exponents congruent mod \(502\) combine. Hence the remainder has the form
\[
(1+x)^{10000}\equiv \sum_{r=0}^{501} S_r x^r \pmod{x^{502}-1},
\]
so \(S_r\) is exactly the coefficient of \(x^r\) in the remainder.

Now work modulo \(503\). Over \(\mathbb F_{503}\), the polynomial \(x^{502}-1\) factors as
\[
x^{502}-1=\prod_{a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times}(x-a),
\]
so two polynomials are congruent mod \(x^{502}-1\) iff they agree on all \(a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times\).

For any \(a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times\):
- If \(1+a=0\), then \((1+a)^{10000}=0=(1+a)^{462}\).
- If \(1+a\neq 0\), then by Fermat, \((1+a)^{502}=1\), so
\[
(1+a)^{10000}=(1+a)^{10000\bmod 502}=(1+a)^{462}.
\]
Thus \((1+a)^{10000}=(1+a)^{462}\) for every \(a\in\mathbb F_{503}^\times\), which implies
\[
(1+x)^{10000}\equiv (1+x)^{462}\pmod{503,\ x^{502}-1}.
\]

But \((1+x)^{462}\) already has degree \(462<502\), so it is itself the remainder modulo \(x^{502}-1\). Therefore, modulo \(503\),
\[
S_r \equiv 
\begin{cases}
\binom{462}{r} & 0\le r\le 462,\\
0 & 463\le r\le 501.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(503\) is prime and \(503>462\), none of the binomial coefficients \(\binom{462}{r}\) (for \(0\le r\le 462\)) are divisible by \(503\). Hence \(S_r\) is divisible by \(503\) exactly for \(r=463,464,\dots,501\), which is
\[
501-463+1=39
\]
values.

\boxed{39}

Let \(p=503\). Work modulo \(p\).

### 1) Package the \(S_r\) as coefficients mod \(x^{502}-1\)
Consider
\[
(1+x)^{10000}=\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}x^k .
\]
Reducing modulo \(x^{502}-1\) (so \(x^{502}\equiv 1\)), every term \(x^{502m+r}\) becomes \(x^r\). Hence in \(\mathbb{F}_p[x]/(x^{502}-1)\),
\[
(1+x)^{10000}\equiv \sum_{r=0}^{501}\left(\sum_{m\ge 0}\binom{10000}{502m+r}\right)x^r
= \sum_{r=0}^{501} S_r x^r.
\]
So the reduced polynomial of degree \(<502\),
\[
Q(x):=\sum_{r=0}^{501} S_r x^r \in \mathbb{F}_p[x],
\]
satisfies
\[
Q(x)\equiv (1+x)^{10000}\pmod{x^{502}-1}.
\]

### 2) Evaluate on all roots of \(x^{502}-1\) in \(\mathbb{F}_{503}\)
In \(\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\), every nonzero \(a\) satisfies \(a^{502}=1\), so the roots of \(x^{502}-1\) are exactly the \(502\) nonzero field elements. Also, \(x^{502}-1\) has distinct roots since its derivative is \(502x^{501}\not\equiv 0\pmod{503}\).

For any \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\),
\[
Q(a)=(1+a)^{10000}.
\]
If \(1+a\neq 0\), then by Fermat \((1+a)^{502}=1\), so
\[
(1+a)^{10000}=(1+a)^{10000\bmod 502}=(1+a)^{462},
\]
since \(10000=502\cdot 19+462\).
If \(a=-1\), then both sides are \(0\) anyway. Thus for all \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\),
\[
Q(a)=(1+a)^{462}.
\]

Now \((1+x)^{462}\) has degree \(462<502\). Both \(Q(x)\) and \((1+x)^{462}\) have degree \(<502\) and agree on all \(502\) distinct points \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\), so they must be identical polynomials in \(\mathbb{F}_{503}[x]\):
\[
Q(x)=(1+x)^{462}.
\]

### 3) Read off coefficients modulo \(503\)
Therefore, for \(0\le r\le 501\),
\[
S_r \equiv [x^r](1+x)^{462}=
\begin{cases}
\binom{462}{r} & 0\le r\le 462,\\
0 & 463\le r\le 501,
\end{cases}
\pmod{503}.
\]

Since \(462<503\), none of the binomial coefficients \(\binom{462}{r}\) (with \(0\le r\le 462\)) is divisible by \(503\): in \(\mathbb{F}_{503}\), \(\binom{462}{r}=\dfrac{462!}{r!(462-r)!}\neq 0\) because all factorials involved are products of nonzero residues.

So the only \(S_r\) that are multiples of \(503\) are those with \(463\le r\le 501\), i.e. \(501-463+1=39\) values.

\[
\boxed{39}
\]

Let \(p=503\) (prime) and note that \(502=p-1\).

Define
\[
S_r=\sum_{m\ge0}\binom{10000}{502m+r}\qquad(0\le r\le 501).
\]

### 1) Roots-of-unity filter (mod \(502\))
Let \(\omega\) be a primitive \(502\)-nd root of unity. The standard filter gives
\[
S_r=\frac1{502}\sum_{j=0}^{501}\omega^{-rj}(1+\omega^j)^{10000}.
\]
We will compute this congruence modulo \(503\). In \(\mathbb{F}_{503}\), the multiplicative group \(\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\) has order \(502\), so we can take \(\omega\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\) to be a generator; then \(\{\omega^j:0\le j\le 501\}=\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\).

Thus, working in \(\bmod 503\),
\[
S_r \equiv \frac1{502}\sum_{a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*} a^{-r}(1+a)^{10000}.
\]

### 2) Reduce the exponent \(10000\) modulo \(502\)
For \(a\neq -1\), we have \(1+a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\), so by Fermat/Euler in \(\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\),
\[
(1+a)^{502}=1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad (1+a)^{10000}=(1+a)^{10000\bmod 502}.
\]
Compute \(10000 \bmod 502\): \(502\cdot 19=9538\), remainder \(462\). Hence
\[
(1+a)^{10000}\equiv (1+a)^{462}\quad (a\neq -1).
\]
If \(a=-1\), then \((1+a)^{10000}=0\), so the same formula still holds for the sum (that term contributes \(0\) anyway). Therefore
\[
S_r \equiv \frac1{502}\sum_{a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*} a^{-r}(1+a)^{462}\pmod{503}.
\]

### 3) Expand and use power-sum orthogonality
Expand:
\[
(1+a)^{462}=\sum_{k=0}^{462}\binom{462}{k}a^k.
\]
So
\[
S_r \equiv \frac1{502}\sum_{k=0}^{462}\binom{462}{k}\sum_{a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*} a^{k-r}.
\]
In \(\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*\) (a cyclic group of order \(502\)),
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb{F}_{503}^\*} a^t=
\begin{cases}
502,& 502\mid t,\\
0,& 502\nmid t.
\end{cases}
\]
Now \(k\in[0,462]\) and \(r\in[0,501]\). The congruence \(k-r\equiv 0\pmod{502}\) can only happen when \(k=r\) (since \(k-r\) lies between \(-501\) and \(462\)). Thus:
- If \(0\le r\le 462\), only the term \(k=r\) survives, giving
  \[
  S_r \equiv \frac1{502}\binom{462}{r}\cdot 502 \equiv \binom{462}{r}\pmod{503}.
  \]
- If \(463\le r\le 501\), no \(k\) matches, so
  \[
  S_r \equiv 0\pmod{503}.
  \]

### 4) Determine when \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\)
For \(0\le r\le 462\), we have \(S_r\equiv \binom{462}{r}\pmod{503}\). Since \(503>462\), the prime \(503\) does not divide \(462!\), hence cannot divide any \(\binom{462}{r}\). So none of these are \(0\pmod{503}\).

For \(463\le r\le 501\), all \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\). The count is
\[
501-463+1=39.
\]

\boxed{39}
\]

Let \(p=503\). Note that \(502=p-1\).

For \(0\le r\le 501\),
\[
S_r=\sum_{m\ge 0}\binom{10000}{502m+r}.
\]
Reduce modulo \(p\). In \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), consider
\[
(1+x)^{10000}=\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}x^k.
\]
Work in the quotient ring
\[
R=\mathbb F_p[x]/(x^{502}-1).
\]
In \(R\), we have \(x^{502}=1\), so for any \(k\),
\[
x^k \equiv x^{\,k\bmod 502}.
\]
Therefore the remainder of \((1+x)^{10000}\) upon reduction modulo \(x^{502}-1\) is
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{501} (S_r \bmod p)\,x^r,
\]
since the coefficient of \(x^r\) collects exactly the terms with exponents \(k\equiv r\pmod{502}\).

Now use the “Freshman’s dream” in characteristic \(p\):
\[
(1+x)^{503} \equiv 1+x^{503}\quad \text{in }\mathbb F_p[x].
\]
But in \(R\), \(x^{503}=x^{502}x\equiv x\). Hence in \(R\),
\[
(1+x)^{503}\equiv 1+x.
\]
Write \(10000=503\cdot 19+443\). Then in \(R\),
\[
(1+x)^{10000}=(1+x)^{503\cdot 19}(1+x)^{443}\equiv\bigl((1+x)^{503}\bigr)^{19}(1+x)^{443}\equiv(1+x)^{19}(1+x)^{443}=(1+x)^{462}.
\]
Since \(462<502\), this polynomial already has degree \(<502\), so it is exactly the remainder. Thus for \(0\le r\le 501\),
\[
S_r \equiv [x^r](1+x)^{462}=
\begin{cases}
\binom{462}{r} & 0\le r\le 462,\\
0 & 463\le r\le 501,
\end{cases}
\pmod{503}.
\]

Now \(\binom{462}{r}\) is **not** divisible by \(503\) for any \(0\le r\le 462\), because \(462<p\) implies all binomial coefficients \(\binom{462}{r}\) are nonzero modulo \(p\).

Therefore, \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\) occurs exactly for
\[
r=463,464,\dots,501,
\]
which is \(501-463+1=39\) values.

Let
\[
P(x)=(1+x)^{10000}=\sum_{k=0}^{10000}\binom{10000}{k}x^k.
\]
Reducing exponents modulo \(502\) corresponds to working in the quotient ring \(\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{502}-1)\). In that ring,
\[
P(x)\equiv \sum_{r=0}^{501} S_r x^r \pmod{x^{502}-1},
\]
because each term \(x^{r+502m}\equiv x^r\), so the coefficient of \(x^r\) becomes exactly \(S_r\).

Now reduce modulo \(503\). Work in \(\mathbb F_{503}[x]/(x^{502}-1)\). Since \(503\) is prime, in characteristic \(503\) we have the “Freshman’s dream”
\[
(1+x)^{503} \equiv 1+x^{503}\pmod{503}.
\]
Write
\[
10000=503\cdot 19+443.
\]
Then in \(\mathbb F_{503}[x]\),
\[
(1+x)^{10000}=(1+x)^{503\cdot 19}(1+x)^{443}\equiv (1+x^{503})^{19}(1+x)^{443}.
\]
In the quotient \(\mathbb F_{503}[x]/(x^{502}-1)\), we have \(x^{502}\equiv 1\), hence \(x^{503}=x^{502}\cdot x\equiv x\). Therefore \(1+x^{503}\equiv 1+x\), so
\[
(1+x)^{10000}\equiv (1+x)^{19}(1+x)^{443}=(1+x)^{462}\quad \text{in }\mathbb F_{503}[x]/(x^{502}-1).
\]
But \((1+x)^{462}\) has degree \(462<502\), so no further reduction modulo \(x^{502}-1\) occurs. Hence for \(0\le r\le 501\),
\[
S_r \equiv 
\begin{cases}
\binom{462}{r} \pmod{503}, & 0\le r\le 462,\\[4pt]
0 \pmod{503}, & 463\le r\le 501.
\end{cases}
\]

Finally, since \(503>462\), the prime \(503\) does not divide \(462!\), so it cannot divide any \(\binom{462}{r}\) (a ratio of integers not divisible by \(503\)). Thus:
- For \(0\le r\le 462\), \(S_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{503}\).
- For \(463\le r\le 501\), \(S_r\equiv 0\pmod{503}\).

The number of integers \(r\) with \(463\le r\le 501\) is
\[
501-463+1=39.

Let \(n=10000\) and \(q=502\). For \(0\le r<502\),
\[
S_r=\sum_{m\ge 0}\binom{n}{qm+r}.
\]

### 1) Roots-of-unity filter in \(\mathbb F_{503}\)
Since \(503\) is prime, the nonzero elements of \(\mathbb F_{503}\) form a cyclic group of order \(502\). Let \(g\) be a primitive root mod \(503\), so the \(502\)-nd roots of unity in \(\mathbb F_{503}\) are \(1,g,g^2,\dots,g^{501}\).

The standard filter gives
\[
S_r=\frac1{502}\sum_{j=0}^{501} g^{-jr}(1+g^j)^{10000}
\]
as an identity in any field containing the \(502\)-nd roots of unity, hence also modulo \(503\).

Modulo \(503\), we have \(502\equiv -1\), so \(\frac1{502}\equiv -1\pmod{503}\). Thus
\[
S_r \equiv -\sum_{j=0}^{501} g^{-jr}(1+g^j)^{10000}\pmod{503}.

\[
(1+x)^{503}\equiv 1+x^{503}\pmod{503}.

\[
(1+x)^{10000}=(1+x)^{443}\left((1+x)^{503}\right)^{19}\equiv (1+x)^{443}(1+x^{503})^{19}\pmod{503}.

\[

\[

\]
Equiangular and closed means the vectors sum to \(0\):
\[
a_1+a_2\omega+a_3\omega^2+a_4\omega^3+a_5\omega^4=0. \tag{1}
\]

### 1) Use diagonal squares to find the adjacent product sum
A diagonal from vertex \(i\) to \(i+2\) equals the vector sum of two consecutive sides, so its squared length is
\[
|a_i + a_{i+1}\omega|^2 = a_i^2+a_{i+1}^2+2a_ia_{i+1}\cos72^\circ.
\]
Summing over the 5 diagonals gives
\[
800 = \sum_{i=1}^5 (a_i^2+a_{i+1}^2) + 2\cos72^\circ\sum_{i=1}^5 a_i a_{i+1}.
\]
But \(\sum (a_i^2+a_{i+1}^2)=2\sum a_i^2 =2\cdot 308=616\). Hence
\[
800=616+2\cos72^\circ\,S,\quad S:=\sum_{i=1}^5 a_i a_{i+1}.
\]
So
\[
S=\frac{184}{2\cos72^\circ}=\frac{92}{\cos72^\circ}.
\]
Using \(\cos72^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\),
\[
S=92\cdot \frac{4}{\sqrt5-1}=92(\sqrt5+1). \tag{2}

\[

- adjacent pairs (difference \(1\) or \(4\)): cosine \(\cos72^\circ\), sum \(S\),
- non-adjacent pairs (difference \(2\) or \(3\)): cosine \(\cos144^\circ\), sum \(N:=\sum_{i=1}^5 a_i a_{i+2}\).

\[

\]

\[
2\cos72^\circ\,S = 2\cos72^\circ\cdot \frac{92}{\cos72^\circ}=184.
\]

\[
0=308+184+2\cos144^\circ\,N \implies 2\cos144^\circ\,N=-492.
\]
Since \(\cos144^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt5+1}{4}\), we have \(2\cos144^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}\), hence
\[
-\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}N=-492 \implies N=\frac{984}{\sqrt5+1}=246(\sqrt5-1). \tag{3}

Each diagonal connects vertices two apart, so it equals the sum of two consecutive side vectors, e.g. \(\overrightarrow{V_0V_2}=a\mathbf{u}_0+b\mathbf{u}_1\). Thus
\[
|a\mathbf{u}_0+b\mathbf{u}_1|^2 = a^2+b^2+2ab\cos72^\circ.
\]
Summing over all 5 diagonals gives
\[
800 = 2(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2) + 2\cos72^\circ\,(ab+bc+cd+de+ea).
\]
Using (1):
\[
800 = 2\cdot 308 + 2\cos72^\circ\,T
\]
where \(T=ab+bc+cd+de+ea\). Hence
\[
184 = 2\cos72^\circ\,T \quad\Rightarrow\quad T=\frac{92}{\cos72^\circ}.
\]
Since \(\cos72^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\),
\[
T=\frac{92}{(\sqrt5-1)/4}=92(\sqrt5+1)=92\sqrt5+92. \tag{2}
\]

### 2) Use the closure condition to find the nonadjacent pair sum
Let
\[
U=ac+bd+ce+da+eb
\]
(the 5 nonadjacent pairs).

Take squared magnitude of the closure vector sum:
\[
0=\left|a\mathbf{u}_0+b\mathbf{u}_1+c\mathbf{u}_2+d\mathbf{u}_3+e\mathbf{u}_4\right|^2.
\]
Expanding via dot products, pairs at angle \(72^\circ\) contribute \(\cos72^\circ\) and pairs at angle \(144^\circ\) contribute \(\cos144^\circ\):
\[
0=(a^2+\cdots+e^2)+2\cos72^\circ\,T+2\cos144^\circ\,U.
\]
Plug in \(a^2+\cdots+e^2=308\) and compute \(2\cos72^\circ\,T\). From (2),
\[
2\cos72^\circ\,T = 2\cdot \frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\cdot 92(\sqrt5+1)
= \frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}\cdot 92(\sqrt5+1)
= \frac{92}{2}\cdot 4 = 184.
\]
So
\[
0=308+184+2\cos144^\circ\,U \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2\cos144^\circ\,U=-492.
\]
Since \(\cos144^\circ=-\cos36^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt5+1}{4}\),
\[
U=\frac{-492}{2\cos144^\circ}=\frac{-492}{2\cdot (-(\sqrt5+1)/4)}
=246(\sqrt5-1)=246\sqrt5-246. \tag{3}
\]

### 3) Compute the perimeter squared
Let \(P=a+b+c+d+e\). Then
\[
P^2=(a^2+\cdots+e^2)+2\sum_{1\le i<j\le 5} a_i a_j.
\]
All \(\binom52=10\) products split into 5 adjacent (\(T\)) and 5 nonadjacent (\(U\)), so
\[
\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j = T+U.
\]
Thus
\[
P^2=308+2(T+U).
\]
Using (2) and (3):
\[
T+U=(92\sqrt5+92)+(246\sqrt5-246)=338\sqrt5-154,
\]
so
\[
P^2=308+2(338\sqrt5-154)=308+676\sqrt5-308=676\sqrt5.
\]
Therefore \(P^2=m\sqrt n\) with \(m=676,\ n=5\), and
\[
m+n=676+5=681.
\]

Let \(S\) be a finite set of integers. A cousin \(T\) corresponds exactly to choosing, for each \(s\in S\), a distinct integer \(t\notin S\) with \(|t-s|=1\). Equivalently, we choose a matching in the integer line graph that matches every vertex of \(S\) to a neighbor outside \(S\).

---

## 1) Split by parity
Even elements of \(S\) can only be paired with odd elements of \(T\), and odd elements of \(S\) can only be paired with even elements of \(T\). These two parts use disjoint sets of \(T\)-vertices (odd vs. even), so the choices are independent. Hence
\[
\#\{\text{cousins of }S\} \;=\; C_{\text{even}}\cdot C_{\text{odd}},
\]
where \(C_{\text{even}}\) counts valid matchings from \(S\cap 2\mathbb Z\) to odd integers \(\notin S\), and similarly for \(C_{\text{odd}}\).

Since \(4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101\) is divisible by the prime \(101\), at least one of \(C_{\text{even}},C_{\text{odd}}\) is divisible by \(101\). WLOG, \(101\mid C_{\text{even}}\).

---

## 2) The even part breaks into “\(\pm 1\)” chains and each chain contributes \(\le r+1\)
List the even elements of \(S\) in increasing order. Two even elements can only “interact” (compete for the same odd neighbor) if they differ by \(2\), because then they share the middle odd integer.

Thus the even elements decompose into disjoint maximal chains of the form
\[
x,\ x+2,\ x+4,\ \dots,\ x+2(r-1).
\]
Consider one such chain of length \(r\). If none of the odd integers between them are in \(S\), then for each \(k=0,1,\dots,r\) we can pair the first \(k\) evens to their left odd neighbors and the remaining \(r-k\) evens to their right odd neighbors; these are all valid and distinct, giving exactly \(r+1\) matchings.

If some odd integer is forbidden (belongs to \(S\)), that only removes options, so **the number of matchings contributed by any length-\(r\) chain is at most \(r+1\).**

Therefore \(C_{\text{even}}\) is a product of integers, each \(\le r_i+1\) for some chain length \(r_i\), and in particular every prime divisor of \(C_{\text{even}}\) is \(\le \max(r_i+1)\).

Since \(101\mid C_{\text{even}}\), some chain must have \(r+1\ge 101\), hence \(r\ge 100\). So
\[
|S|\ge |S\cap 2\mathbb Z|\ge 100.
\]

Moreover, because \(101\) is prime, the only way to get a factor \(101\) from a product of integers \(\le r+1\) is to have an actual factor \(101\), i.e. to have a chain with \(r+1=101\), so \(r=100\). That chain already uses \(100\) elements of \(S\).

So the remaining multiplicative factor needed is
\[
\frac{4040}{101}=40.
\]

---

## 3) Minimizing how many extra elements are needed to get a factor \(40\)
Any additional chain of length \(r\) contributes at most \(r+1\) cousins and costs \(r\) elements of \(S\). So to multiply the number of cousins by \(40\), we must write \(40\) as a product
\[
40 = a_1a_2\cdots a_m,\qquad a_i\ge 2,
\]
where each factor \(a_i\) comes from some chain and costs at least \(a_i-1\) elements (since \(a_i\le r_i+1\Rightarrow r_i\ge a_i-1\)). Thus the total number of extra elements needed is at least
\[
(a_1-1)+\cdots+(a_m-1).
\]

We claim the minimum possible is \(7\). Check all possibilities with total “cost” \(\le 6\): write \(6\) as a sum of \(b_i=a_i-1\ge 1\), so \(a_i=b_i+1\), and compute \(\prod (b_i+1)\). The partitions of \(6\) give products:
- \(6\to 7\)
- \(5+1\to 6\cdot2=12\)
- \(4+2\to 5\cdot3=15\)
- \(4+1+1\to 5\cdot2\cdot2=20\)
- \(3+3\to 4\cdot4=16\)
- \(3+2+1\to 4\cdot3\cdot2=24\)
- \(3+1+1+1\to 4\cdot2^3=32\)
- \(2+2+2\to 3^3=27\)
- \(2+2+1+1\to 3\cdot3\cdot2\cdot2=36\)
- \(2+1+1+1+1\to 3\cdot2^4=48\)
- \(1+1+1+1+1+1\to 2^6=64\)

None equals \(40\). Hence cost \(\ge 7\). And cost \(7\) is achievable via
\[
40 = 5\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2,
\]
with cost \((5-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)=4+1+1+1=7\).

Therefore, beyond the \(100\) elements needed to create the factor \(101\), we need at least \(7\) more elements to create the factor \(40\). So
\[
|S|\ge 100+7=107.
\]

---

## 4) Construction with \(|S|=107\) and exactly \(4040\) cousins
Take \(S\) to consist only of even integers, in four separated chains:

- Chain of length \(100\): \(0,2,4,\dots,198\)  (contributes \(101\))
- Chain of length \(4\): \(202,204,206,208\) (contributes \(5\))
- Three isolated evens: \(300,400,500\) (each contributes \(2\))

These parts are far apart so they do not share any odd neighbors, hence their counts multiply:
\[
101\cdot 5\cdot 2^3 \;=\; 4040.
\]
Thus \(S\) has exactly \(4040\) cousins with \(|S|=107\).

---

### 1) Reformulate “cousins” as matchings
Fix a finite set \(S\subset\mathbb Z\). A set \(T\) is a cousin of \(S\) iff there is a bijection (pairing) \(S\to T\) such that each \(s\in S\) is paired with either \(s-1\) or \(s+1\), and \(T\cap S=\varnothing\).

Equivalently, build a graph whose vertices are integers and whose edges connect consecutive integers. We only allow an edge \(\{s,t\}\) to be used if \(s\in S\), \(t\notin S\), and \(|s-t|=1\). Then a cousin \(T\) corresponds exactly to a matching that covers every vertex of \(S\): each \(s\in S\) is matched to a distinct neighbor \(t\notin S\), and \(T\) is the set of all matched \(t\)’s.

So:

\[
\#\{\text{cousins of }S\}=\#\{\text{matchings that saturate }S\}.
\]

Also, since this graph is a subgraph of the integer line, every connected component is a path, and if such a matching exists on a component, it is forced locally once endpoints are decided; different components contribute independently (products).

---

### 2) What do connected components look like?
Consider the graph \(G\) whose vertices are
\[
V = S\ \cup\ \{x\in\mathbb Z\setminus S:\ \text{\(x\) is adjacent to some }s\in S\},
\]
with edges between consecutive integers \(\{n,n+1\}\) **only when exactly one endpoint lies in \(S\)** (since \(T\) must be disjoint from \(S\)).

Key observations:

- If \(s,s+1\in S\), then there is **no** edge between them (both in \(S\)), so adjacency in \(S\) actually *splits* components. Moreover, such an endpoint \(s\) has only one available neighbor outside \(S\), making its match forced.
- If two elements of \(S\) differ by \(\ge 3\), their neighbor-sets \(\{s\pm1\}\) are disjoint, so they lie in different components and act independently.
- The only way two elements of \(S\) interact is when they differ by \(2\), because then they share a common candidate neighbor.

Therefore, any component that contributes more than \(1\) matching must consist of numbers of a single parity spaced by \(2\), i.e. a chain
\[
S_{\text{comp}}=\{a,a+2,a+4,\dots,a+2(k-1)\}
\]
with **no adjacent elements of \(S\)**.

---

### 3) Cousins contributed by a \(2\)-spaced chain
Let
\[
S_{\text{comp}}=\{a,a+2,\dots,a+2(k-1)\}.
\]
The possible partner vertices (outside \(S\)) in this component are
\[
\{a-1,\,a+1,\,a+3,\,\dots,\,a+2k-1\},
\]
which are \(k+1\) vertices. Each \(s=a+2(i-1)\) is adjacent exactly to the two consecutive candidates \(a+2i-3\) and \(a+2i-1\).

A matching saturating all \(k\) vertices of \(S_{\text{comp}}\) must choose \(k\) distinct partners among these \(k+1\) candidates, i.e. it leaves exactly one candidate unused. And in a path, once you choose which candidate is unused, the matching is forced (endpoints force inward).

Hence the number of cousins contributed by this component is exactly
\[
k+1.
\]

Components that arise from adjacent elements in \(S\) contribute exactly \(1\) (forced), so they never help minimize \(|S|\) for a fixed large cousin count.

Thus, for an optimal (minimum-size) \(S\), we may assume \(S\) is a disjoint union of \(2\)-spaced chains, and the total number of cousins is a product of \((k_i+1)\)’s.

---

### 4) Force a factor \(101\)
We are told \(S\) has exactly
\[
4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101
\]
cousins. Since \(101\) is prime, in the product \(\prod (k_i+1)\), some factor must be divisible by \(101\). The smallest possibility is \(k_i+1=101\), i.e.
\[
k_i=100.
\]
So any such \(S\) must have at least \(100\) elements.

---

### 5) Minimize extra elements to supply the remaining factor \(40\)
After taking a \(100\)-element chain giving \(101\) cousins, we need the remaining factor
\[
\frac{4040}{101}=40.
\]
We want to write \(40\) as a product of integers \(\ge 2\) while minimizing \(\sum (f_j-1)\), because each factor \(f_j\) corresponds to a chain of length \(f_j-1\).

Best factorization:
\[
40=5\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2,
\]
which uses \((5-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)=4+1+1+1=7\) elements.

So the minimum total is
\[
100+7=107.
\]

---

### 6) Construction achieving \(107\)
Take disjoint chains far apart, e.g.
- \(A=\{0,2,4,\dots,198\}\) (100 elements) \(\Rightarrow 101\) cousins,
- \(B=\{300,302,304,306\}\) (4 elements) \(\Rightarrow 5\) cousins,
- singletons \(\{400\},\{500\},\{600\}\) \(\Rightarrow 2\) cousins each.

They are separated by at least \(3\), so counts multiply:
\[
101\cdot 5\cdot 2^3 = 4040.
\]
Total elements \(=100+4+1+1+1=107\).

Therefore the least possible size of \(S\) is \(\boxed{107}\).

View a cousin \(T\) of \(S\) as choosing, for each \(s\in S\), one of the integers \(s-1\) or \(s+1\), in such a way that

- all chosen integers are distinct (so we really get a set \(T\)), and  
- none of them lies in \(S\) (automatic if we only choose \(\pm1\) and require disjointness).

Equivalently, build a graph on the integer line where we draw an edge between \(s\in S\) and any \(t\notin S\) with \(|s-t|=1\). A cousin \(T\) corresponds exactly to a matching that covers all vertices of \(S\); then \(T\) is the set of matched neighbors.

---

### 1) Components multiply
If \(S\) splits into parts that are at distance \(\ge 3\) from each other, then their neighbor sets \(\{x\pm1\}\) are disjoint, so matchings (hence cousins) can be chosen independently on each part. Therefore the number of cousins of \(S\) is the product of the numbers of cousins of its distance-\(\ge3\) components.

So we reduce to understanding a **connected component** of \(S\), meaning consecutive elements of that component differ by at most \(2\).

---

### 2) A connected component with consecutive integers has only 1 cousin
If a component contains consecutive integers \(x,x+1\in S\), then \(x\) cannot match to \(x+1\) (since \(T\cap S=\varnothing\)), so \(x\) must match to \(x-1\). Similarly \(x+1\) must match to \(x+2\). This forces the usage of \(x-1\) and \(x+2\), and if the component extends further, those forced choices propagate outward, eliminating all freedom. One checks inductively along the line that **there is at most one way** to match every element of that component. Hence:

- any connected component containing a consecutive pair contributes a factor \(1\) to the cousin count.

Such components only increase \(|S|\) without increasing the number of cousins, so a smallest \(S\) with 4040 cousins will have **no consecutive integers**.

---

### 3) Connected components with no consecutive integers are “every-other-integer chains”
In a connected component with no consecutive integers, the only allowed gap between successive elements is \(2\). Thus every such component has the form
\[
\{a,a+2,a+4,\dots,a+2(k-1)\}
\]
for some \(k\ge1\). Call its cousin count \(f(k)\).

**Claim:** \(f(k)=k+1\).

*Proof by recursion.* For the leftmost element \(a\), either

- it matches to \(a-1\). Then the remaining \(k-1\) elements form the same type of chain, giving \(f(k-1)\) choices; or
- it matches to \(a+1\). Then \(a+1\) is no longer available, forcing \(a+2\) to match to \(a+3\), which forces \(a+4\) to match to \(a+5\), etc., yielding exactly \(1\) choice.

So \(f(k)=f(k-1)+1\), with \(f(1)=2\). Hence \(f(k)=k+1\). ∎

Therefore, if \(S\) is a disjoint union of such chains of sizes \(k_1,k_2,\dots,k_m\) (separated by gaps \(\ge3\)), then
\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\prod_{i=1}^m (k_i+1),\qquad |S|=\sum_{i=1}^m k_i.
\]

Let \(x_i=k_i+1\ge2\). Then
\[

Model cousins as matchings on the integer line.

**1) Cousins = matchings that saturate \(S\).**  
Given a finite set \(S\subset\mathbb Z\), let \(N\) be the set of integers not in \(S\) that are adjacent to some element of \(S\) (i.e. differ by \(1\)). Consider the bipartite graph \(G\) with left part \(S\), right part \(N\), and edges \(s\!-\!n\) when \(|s-n|=1\).

A cousin \(T\) of \(S\) is exactly the image of a choice, for each \(s\in S\), of one adjacent integer \(n=s\pm1\) such that:
- all chosen \(n\)’s are distinct (so \(T\) is a set of size \(|S|\)),
- all chosen \(n\)’s lie outside \(S\) (so \(T\cap S=\varnothing\)).

That is exactly a **matching in \(G\) that matches every vertex of \(S\)**. So:
\[
\#\{\text{cousins of }S\}=\#\{\text{matchings in }G\text{ saturating }S\}.
\]

**2) Each connected component contributes independently (product rule).**  
The graph \(G\) is a disjoint union of connected components; choices of matchings on different components are independent. Hence the total number of cousins is the product of the numbers of saturating matchings on each component.

**3) Classify connected components of \(G\).**  
Because edges only connect consecutive integers, every component of \(G\) is a path along the number line. Also, along such a component, vertices alternate between \(S\) and \(N\) (since edges only go between \(S\) and \(\mathbb Z\setminus S\)).

Let a component have \(k\) vertices from \(S\). Then along the line it must look like either

- **Type A (ends in \(N\)):**
\[
n_0 - s_1 - n_1 - s_2 - \cdots - s_k - n_k
\]
which has \(k+1\) vertices on the \(N\) side, or

- **Type B (an end in \(S\)):**
\[
s_1 - n_1 - s_2 - \cdots - s_k
\quad\text{(or the reverse)}
\]
which has exactly \(k\) vertices on the \(N\) side.

Now count saturating matchings:

- In **Type A**, matching all \(k\) vertices of \(S\) means choosing \(k\) distinct \(n_i\)’s out of the \(k+1\) available, with adjacency forcing a unique matching once you decide **which single \(n_i\)** is left unused. Therefore, the number of saturating matchings is exactly
\[
k+1.
\]

- In **Type B**, Hall’s condition forces the matching to use every \(N\)-vertex, and the path structure forces a **unique** saturating matching (if it exists). So the component contributes exactly \(1\).

**4) No Type B components in a size-minimal solution.**  
If a component contributes \(1\), then in every cousin \(T\) the corresponding matched \(N\)-vertices are forced. Removing that entire forced component from \(S\) removes the same forced vertices from every cousin \(T\), giving a bijection between cousins before/after removal. So the number of cousins stays \(4040\) but \(|S|\) decreases—contradicting minimality.  
Hence, in a minimum-size \(S\), **every component must be Type A**, contributing a factor \(k_i+1\) while using \(k_i\) elements of \(S\).

So we must write
\[
4040=\prod_{i=1}^m (k_i+1),
\qquad |S|=\sum_{i=1}^m k_i=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl((k_i+1)-1\bigr).
\]
Let \(f_i=k_i+1\ge2\). Then
\[
4040=\prod f_i,\qquad |S|=\sum (f_i-1).
\]

Key inequality: for integers \(a,b\ge2\),
\[
(ab-1) - \bigl((a-1)+(b-1)\bigr)=(a-1)(b-1)>0,
\]
so **splitting a composite factor strictly decreases** the sum \(\sum(f_i-1)\). Therefore the minimum occurs when all \(f_i\) are prime factors of \(4040\).

\[
4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101.
\]
Thus the minimum size is
\[
|S|=3\cdot(2-1)+(5-1)+(101-1)=3+4+100=107.
\]

\[
101\cdot 5\cdot 2^3=4040,

and total elements \(100+4+3=107\).

## 1) Structural restriction on \(S\)
If \(s-1\in S\) and \(s+1\in S\), then \(s\) has no available partner outside \(S\) differing by \(1\). Hence:

- No element of \(S\) can have both neighbors in \(S\).
- In particular, \(S\) contains no three consecutive integers.

So consecutive elements of \(S\) occur only in blocks of size \(1\) or \(2\).

---

## 2) Decomposing into independent components
If two elements of \(S\) are at distance \(\ge 3\), then they do not compete for any possible partner (their \(\pm1\) neighborhoods are disjoint). Thus the choices for matchings (and hence cousin sets) multiply across such separated groups.

So we may decompose \(S\) into components where successive elements differ by at most \(2\). The total number of cousins is the product of the numbers of cousins coming from each component.

---

## 3) Counting cousins for one component
Consider one such component \(C\subseteq S\) with \(|C|=k\). Let
\[
N(C)=\{x\notin S:\ \exists s\in C\text{ with }|x-s|=1\}
\]
be the available neighbor integers (possible \(T\)-elements) adjacent to \(C\).

A cousin-matching on this component is exactly an injective choice of one neighbor in \(N(C)\) for each \(s\in C\). Hence we need \(|N(C)|\ge k\).

### (a) If the component contains an adjacent pair \(s,s+1\in C\)
Then \(s\) can only match to \(s-1\) and \(s+1\) can only match to \(s+2\). This forces those choices, and in fact forces outward choices for any nearby elements; one checks this yields **exactly 1** way on that component.

So any component containing an adjacent pair contributes a factor \(1\) to the cousin count, and thus is useless if we want to minimize \(|S|\) for a fixed total number of cousins.

### (b) The useful case: no adjacencies in the component
Then all gaps inside the component must be exactly \(2\) (otherwise the component would split), so the component has the form
\[
C=\{a,a+2,a+4,\dots,a+2(k-1)\}.
\]
Its available neighbors are
\[
N(C)=\{a-1,a+1,a+3,\dots,a+2k-1\},
\]
which has size \(k+1\).

In any injective assignment of neighbors, exactly one element of \(N(C)\) is unused. Conversely, choosing which neighbor is unused forces a unique matching by “greedily” matching from one end. Therefore:

\[
\#(\text{cousins contributed by this component})=k+1.
\]

---

## 4) Therefore, total cousin count has the form \(\prod (k_i+1)\)
To get many cousins efficiently, \(S\) should be a disjoint union of components of the gap-2 type above, with sizes \(k_1,k_2,\dots,k_m\), giving
\[
\#\text{cousins}=\prod_{i=1}^m (k_i+1).
\]
We are told this product equals \(4040\). Let \(f_i=k_i+1\ge 2\). Then
\[
\prod f_i=4040,\qquad |S|=\sum k_i=\sum (f_i-1).
\]

To minimize \(\sum(f_i-1)\) for fixed \(\prod f_i\), we should split factors as much as possible: for integers \(a,b\ge 2\),
\[
(ab-1)-\bigl((a-1)+(b-1)\bigr)=ab-a-b+1=(a-1)(b-1)\ge 1,
\]
so replacing a factor \(ab\) by factors \(a\) and \(b\) strictly decreases \(\sum(f_i-1)\).

Hence the minimum occurs when we factor \(4040\) completely into primes:
\[
4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101.
\]
Thus take factors \(f_i\) to be \(2,2,2,5,101\), giving
\[
|S|_{\min}=(2-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)+(5-1)+(101-1)=1+1+1+4+100=107.
\]

Because this graph is a subgraph of the integer line, every connected component is a (finite) path.

## 2. What components can contribute cousins?
Consider one connected component of this graph. Along the integer line, vertices in the component must alternate between
\[
\mathbb Z\setminus S,\ S,\ \mathbb Z\setminus S,\ S,\ \dots
\]
(since edges only go between \(S\) and \(\mathbb Z\setminus S\)).

Suppose the component contains \(k\) vertices of \(S\). Let the number of \(\mathbb Z\setminus S\) vertices in the component be \(r\). Since the component is an alternating path, necessarily \(r\in\{k-1,k,k+1\}\).

- If \(r\le k-1\), there are fewer available partners than elements of \(S\), so **no** matching can cover all of \(S\).
- If \(r=k\), then there is exactly one matching covering all \(S\) (forced from one end).
- The flexible case is \(r=k+1\): the path starts and ends in \(\mathbb Z\setminus S\). Then:

### Lemma: If a component is an alternating path with \(k\) \(S\)-vertices and \(k+1\) \((\mathbb Z\setminus S)\)-vertices, it contributes exactly \(k+1\) cousins.
**Reason.** In any matching covering all \(k\) \(S\)-vertices, exactly one of the \(k+1\) \((\mathbb Z\setminus S)\)-vertices is left unmatched. Conversely, choosing which \((\mathbb Z\setminus S)\)-vertex is left unmatched forces a unique matching (propagating choices along the path). Hence \(k+1\) matchings.

So, for each “good” component containing \(k\) elements of \(S\), the number of choices contributed is exactly \(k+1\).

Since components are disjoint, the total number of cousins is the product over components:
\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\prod_{i}(k_i+1),

### 1) Independence when elements are far apart

So if \(S\) splits into parts that are separated by gaps \(\ge 3\), then the possible partner sets \(\{s\pm1\}\) from different parts are disjoint, hence choices don’t interact. Therefore:

- If \(S = S_1\cup S_2\) with \(\min_{x\in S_1,y\in S_2}|x-y|\ge 3\), then  
  \[
  \#\text{cousins}(S)=\#\text{cousins}(S_1)\cdot \#\text{cousins}(S_2).
  \]

So we may analyze “components” where consecutive elements differ by at most \(2\).

### 2) Cousin count of one component

Let a component have elements \(a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_m\) with \(a_{i+1}-a_i\in\{1,2\}\).

#### Lemma A: If the component contains a consecutive pair, it has exactly \(1\) cousin.
If \(x,x+1\in S\), then:
- \(x\) cannot pair with \(x+1\) (since \(T\cap S=\varnothing\)), so \(x\) must pair with \(x-1\).
- similarly \(x+1\) must pair with \(x+2\).

Now if there is another element \(x+3\in S\) (the only way to stay in the same component to the right), it cannot use \(x+2\) (already taken), so it must use \(x+4\), and this forcing continues. A similar forcing happens to the left. Hence the entire pairing is forced and unique.

So such a component contributes a factor \(1\) (and is never helpful for minimizing \(|S|\)).

#### Lemma B: If the component has no consecutive pair, then it must be
\[
\{a,\,a+2,\,a+4,\,\dots,\,a+2(m-1)\},
\]
and it has exactly \(m+1\) cousins.
No gap can be \(\ge 3\) inside a component, so all gaps are exactly \(2\).

Let the component be \(a,a+2,\dots,a+2(m-1)\). Any cousin \(T\) must lie in the \(m+1\) “odd” positions
\[
\{a-1,\ a+1,\ a+3,\ \dots,\ a+2m-1\},
\]
and must have size \(m\), so it is this set with exactly one element omitted. Conversely, for each choice of omitted element, there is exactly one way to pair: everything to the left pairs rightward, everything to the right pairs leftward. Hence exactly \(m+1\) cousins.

So every useful component contributes a factor of the form \(m+1\) using \(m\) elements.

### 3) Forcing a factor \(101\)
We are told \(\#\text{cousins}(S)=4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101\), and \(101\) is prime.

By the multiplicativity across separated components, some component must contribute a factor divisible by \(101\).  
By Lemma A, a component with consecutive elements contributes \(1\), not divisible by \(101\).  
So we need a Lemma B component with \(m+1=101\), i.e. \(m=100\).

Thus \(|S|\ge 100\), and we can realize a factor \(101\) using exactly \(100\) elements.

Therefore the minimum possible size is
\[

## 1) Split the problem by parity

Write
\[
S=E\sqcup O,\qquad E=S\cap 2\mathbb Z,\quad O=S\cap(2\mathbb Z+1).
\]
If \(s\in E\) (even), then its partner in \(T\) must be odd; if \(s\in O\), its partner must be even. Hence the choices for even elements and odd elements never compete for the same integer (different parities), so:

\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\#\text{(valid matchings for }E\text{)}\cdot \#\text{(valid matchings for }O\text{)}.
\]

The set \(O\) only affects the counting for \(E\) by possibly *blocking* an even element from using \(s\pm1\) if that neighbor lies in \(O\), and similarly \(E\) can block choices for \(O\). But once \(S\) is fixed, the two counts multiply.

---

## 2) Components within one parity, and the “cut-point” rule

Focus on the even side \(E\). Two even numbers can only try to use the same odd partner if they are distance \(2\) apart:
\[
x,\ x+2\in E \quad\text{both could try to use }x+1.
\]
So in \(E\), the only interactions happen along chains of consecutive even integers spaced by \(2\):
\[
x,\ x+2,\ x+4,\dots, x+2(k-1).
\]
Call such a chain an **even component** of size \(k\). Different even components (separated by at least \(4\)) have disjoint sets of possible odd partners, so their numbers of matchings multiply. The same holds for odd components.

### Key lemma (bound \(k+1\))
In any even component of size \(k\), the number of valid matchings is **at most \(k+1\)**.

**Reason:** label the evens as \(e_1<e_2<\cdots<e_k\) with \(e_{i+1}=e_i+2\). If \(e_i\) is matched to the right (to \(e_i+1\)) and \(e_{i+1}\) is matched to the left (also to \(e_i+1\)), that is a collision. Therefore, in a valid matching you can never have a “right choice” immediately followed by a “left choice.” Thus, as you move along the chain, once you start choosing “right,” you must keep choosing “right.” So a matching is determined by a single cut point \(j\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}\):
- \(e_1,\dots,e_j\) go left,
- \(e_{j+1},\dots,e_k\) go right,

and there are at most \(k+1\) such cut points (some may be disallowed if choices are blocked, but that only decreases the count).

In particular, if no choices are blocked in that component (both directions always available), then **all** \(k+1\) cut points work, so the component contributes exactly \(k+1\) matchings.

## 3) Forcing the prime factor \(101\)

We are told \(\#\text{cousins}(S)=4040\), and
\[
4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101.
\]
Because \(101\) is prime and the total number of cousins is a product of component-counts (even components and odd components), **some single parity component must contribute a factor divisible by \(101\)**.

But a component of size \(k\) contributes \(\le k+1\). For it to be divisible by \(101\), we need
\[
k+1\ge 101 \implies k\ge 100.
\]
So \(|S|\ge 100\).

Moreover, to keep \(|S|\) as small as possible, we should take a component of size exactly \(100\) whose contribution is exactly \(101\) (the smallest possible multiple of \(101\)).

## 4) The remaining factor \(40\) needs at least \(7\) elements

After accounting for a \(101\) factor, we still need a factor
\[
\frac{4040}{101}=40=5\cdot 8.
\]
To get a factor \(5\) from any component, we need some component with contribution \(5\). Since a component of size \(k\) contributes at most \(k+1\), the smallest way to get \(5\) is \(k=4\) with a completely unblocked chain (giving \(k+1=5\)). That uses \(4\) elements.

Separately, to get a factor \(8\), we need at least \(3\) elements each with two independent choices (e.g. three isolated singletons), contributing \(2^3=8\). That uses \(3\) more elements.

So producing a factor \(40\) requires at least \(4+3=7\) elements.

Therefore,
\[
|S|\ \ge\ 100+7\ =\ 107.
\]

### 1) \(S\) cannot contain three consecutive integers
If \(x-1,x,x+1\in S\), then \(x\) can only pair with \(x-1\) or \(x+1\), but those are in \(S\), contradicting \(S\cap T=\varnothing\).  
So \(S\) has no three consecutive integers.

### 2) Split \(S\) into independent components
If two elements of \(S\) differ by at least \(3\), then the possible partners (\(\pm1\)) for one element lie at least \(2\) away from the possible partners of the other, so choices of pairings cannot interfere. Hence the number of cousins multiplies across “components” of \(S\), where a component is a maximal subset of \(S\) in which successive elements differ by \(1\) or \(2\).

So we analyze one component \(C\subseteq S\).

## 3) Components with an adjacent pair contribute only \(1\) cousin
Suppose \(a,a+1\in C\). Then in any cousin \(T\),

- \(a\) cannot pair with \(a+1\), so it must pair with \(a-1\). Thus \(a-1\in T\).
- similarly \(a+1\) must pair with \(a+2\). Thus \(a+2\in T\).

Now if \(C\) continues to the right (to stay in the same component), the next possible element is \(a+3\) (since \(a+2\notin S\)). But \(a+3\) cannot use \(a+2\) (already in \(T\)), so it must pair with \(a+4\), forcing \(a+4\in T\). This forcing propagates through the entire component (and similarly to the left). Therefore:

- either the component is impossible (0 cousins), or
- it has exactly **1** cousin.

Thus, to minimize \(|S|\) for a given positive number of cousins, we should **avoid adjacent elements**, because they add elements but do not increase the cousin count.

So from now on assume \(S\) has **no adjacent integers**.

---

## 4) Components without adjacent elements are \(2\)-spaced arithmetic progressions
In a component, gaps between successive elements are \(\le 2\). If there are no adjacent elements, every gap is exactly \(2\).  
So each component has the form
\[
\{x, x+2, x+4,\dots, x+2(k-1)\}
\]
for some \(k\ge 1\). Call such a component a \(2\)-chain of length \(k\).

### 5) A \(2\)-chain of length \(k\) has exactly \(k+1\) cousins
Let the chain be \(x, x+2,\dots,x+2(k-1)\). The possible partners lie among the \(k+1\) integers
\[
x-1,\ x+1,\ x+3,\ \dots,\ x+2k-1.
\]
In any cousin \(T\), each element of the chain must be paired to one adjacent partner, and partners must be distinct. Since there are \(k\) elements but \(k+1\) possible partner positions, exactly **one** of those \(k+1\) positions is unused, and for each choice of the unused position the matching is forced. Hence there are \(k+1\) cousins.

## 6) Therefore the cousin count factors as \(\prod (k_i+1)\)
Let the \(2\)-chains have lengths \(k_1,\dots,k_m\). Then
\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\prod_{i=1}^m (k_i+1),
\qquad |S|=\sum_{i=1}^m k_i.
\]
We need
\[
\prod (k_i+1)=4040.
\]
Let \(f_i=k_i+1\ge 2\). Then \(|S|=\sum (f_i-1)\) and \(\prod f_i=4040\).

To **minimize** \(\sum (f_i-1)\) for fixed product, we should factor as much as possible: if \(f=ab\) with \(a,b\ge 2\), then
\[
(f-1) - \bigl((a-1)+(b-1)\bigr)
=ab-1-(a+b-2)=(a-1)(b-1)\ge 1,

so replacing \(f\) by \(a,b\) **decreases** the total \(\sum(f_i-1)\).

Thus the minimum occurs when all \(f_i\) are the prime factors of \(4040\):
\[
4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101.

So the optimal component lengths are
\[
k_i = 2-1,2-1,2-1,5-1,101-1 = 1,1,1,4,100,
\]
giving
\[
|S|_{\min}=1+1+1+4+100=107.

### 1) Reformulation as a matching problem
Fix a finite set \(S\subset \mathbb Z\). A set \(T\) is a *cousin* of \(S\) iff we can pair each \(s\in S\) with a distinct \(t\in T\) such that \(|s-t|=1\), and also \(T\cap S=\varnothing\).

Build a bipartite graph \(G\) as follows:

- Left vertices: the elements of \(S\).
- Right vertices: the integers \(\notin S\) that are adjacent (distance \(1\)) to some element of \(S\).
- Edges connect \(s\in S\) to \(x\notin S\) when \(|s-x|=1\).

Then a cousin \(T\) is exactly a choice of a matching in \(G\) that covers every left vertex (every \(s\in S\) is matched), and \(T\) is the set of matched right-vertices.  
So the number of cousins equals the number of left-perfect matchings in \(G\).

Also, \(G\) is a subgraph of the integer line, hence every connected component of \(G\) is a path, and matchings multiply across components. Therefore:

\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\prod_{\text{components }C} \#\text{matchings}(C).
\]

---

### 2) Structure and count for one connected component
Consider one connected component \(C\) of \(G\), and let it contain \(k\) vertices from \(S\) (so \(k\) left-vertices).

**Key observation:** In a connected component, elements of \(S\) must be spaced exactly \(2\) apart along the line (otherwise the component breaks). Concretely, the left vertices in a component must look like
\[
a,\,a+2,\,a+4,\dots, a+2(k-1)
\]
for some integer \(a\). The right vertices are then the interleaving odd/even neighbors:
\[
a-1,\ a+1,\ a+3,\dots,\ a+2k-1
\]
except that an endpoint right-vertex might be missing if it lies in \(S\) (i.e. if \(a-1\in S\) or \(a+2k-1\in S\)).

Thus a component has either:
- \(k+1\) right vertices (both ends “free”), or
- \(k\) right vertices (one end blocked), in which case the matching is forced.

**Lemma (count in a component):** If a component contains \(k\) elements of \(S\), then the number of matchings covering all those \(k\) left vertices is at most \(k+1\). Moreover, when both ends are free (so there are \(k+1\) right vertices), the number is exactly \(k+1\).

*Reason:* In the free-end case the component is the alternating path
\[
v_0 - u_1 - v_1 - u_2 - \cdots - u_k - v_k
\]
(\(u_i\in S\), \(v_j\notin S\)). A matching covering all \(u_i\) must leave exactly one \(v_j\) unmatched. For each choice of the unmatched \(v_j\), there is exactly one way to match all \(u_i\) (forced outward from \(v_j\)). Hence exactly \(k+1\) matchings.

So: **to get a factor \(101\) in the cousin count, some component must have \(k+1\) divisible by \(101\), hence \(k\ge 100\).**

---

### 3) Lower bound on \(|S|\)
We are told \(\#\text{cousins}(S)=4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101\).

Because matchings multiply over components, some component must contribute a factor divisible by \(101\). By the lemma, if a component has \(k\) elements of \(S\), its contribution is \(\le k+1\). Therefore we need
\[
k+1\ge 101 \implies k\ge 100.
\]
So \(|S|\ge 100\), and after extracting the factor \(101\), the remaining factor needed is \(4040/101=40\).

Now we minimize how many *additional* elements are needed to produce a factor \(40\). Any component that contributes a factor \(c\ge 2\) must have at least \(c-1\) elements of \(S\) (since its maximum contribution is \(k+1\)). Thus, if \(40=\prod c_i\), we need at least \(\sum (c_i-1)\) elements.

To minimize \(\sum(c_i-1)\), we should split factors as much as possible: for \(a,b\ge2\),
\[
(ab-1) > (a-1)+(b-1),
\]
so replacing a factor \(ab\) by \(a\) and \(b\) decreases the required element count. Hence the minimum occurs at the prime factorization:
\[
40=2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 5,
\]
which requires at least
\[
(2-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)+(5-1)=1+1+1+4=7
\]
elements.

Therefore,
\[
|S|\ge 100+7=107.
\]

### 1) Rephrase “cousins” as choice of left/right neighbors
Fix a finite set \(S\subset \mathbb Z\). A cousin \(T\) corresponds to choosing, for each \(s\in S\), either \(s-1\) or \(s+1\), so that

- the chosen integers are all distinct, and
- none of them lies in \(S\) (this is automatic if we only ever choose \(\pm 1\) from \(s\), except when \(s\pm 1\in S\), in which case that choice is forbidden).

Thus the number of cousins of \(S\) equals the number of injective functions
\[
f:S\to \mathbb Z\setminus S,\qquad f(s)\in\{s-1,s+1\}.
\]

### 2) Components split multiplicatively when separated by gaps \(\ge 3\)
If \(S=A\sqcup B\) and \(|a-b|\ge 3\) for all \(a\in A, b\in B\), then no target \(a\pm 1\) can ever coincide with a target \(b\pm 1\). So choices for \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, and
\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\#\text{cousins}(A)\cdot \#\text{cousins}(B).
\]
Therefore, if we sort \(S=\{x_1<\dots<x_n\}\) and cut it whenever \(x_{i+1}-x_i\ge 3\), the total cousin count is the product over these “blocks”.

So it suffices to understand a **block** \(B=\{x_1<\dots<x_k\}\) with all gaps \(x_{i+1}-x_i\in\{1,2\}\).

### 3) Key bound for a block: at most \(k+1\) cousins
For a block \(B=\{x_1<\dots<x_k\}\), in any valid choice function \(f\), define direction
\[
d_i=\begin{cases}
L & f(x_i)=x_i-1,\\
R & f(x_i)=x_i+1.
\end{cases}
\]

**Claim:** We can never have \(d_i=R\) and \(d_{i+1}=L\).

- If \(x_{i+1}=x_i+1\), then \(x_i+1\in S\), so \(x_i\) is **forbidden** to choose \(R\). So \(d_i\neq R\).
- If \(x_{i+1}=x_i+2\), then \(x_i\) choosing \(R\) and \(x_{i+1}\) choosing \(L\) both target the same integer \(x_i+1\), violating injectivity.

So the direction sequence \((d_1,\dots,d_k)\) is **nondecreasing** in the sense that once you choose \(R\), you can never later choose \(L\). Hence it is completely determined by a “switch index” \(j\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}\):
\[
d_1=\cdots=d_j=L,\qquad d_{j+1}=\cdots=d_k=R,
\]
subject to any forced-direction restrictions (which can only reduce the number).

Therefore:
\[
\#\text{cousins}(B)\le k+1.
\]

Moreover, equality \(\#\text{cousins}(B)=k+1\) is achieved by the block
\[
B=\{0,2,4,\dots,2(k-1)\},
\]
because all \(k+1\) switch choices are valid there.

### 4) For 4040 cousins, a block must contribute a factor 101
We have
\[
4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101,
\]
and \(101\) is prime. Since the total cousin count is a product of block counts (integers), **some block** must have a cousin count divisible by \(101\), hence at least \(101\).

By the bound above, if a block has \(k\) elements then \(\#\text{cousins}(B)\le k+1\). So we need
\[
k+1\ge 101 \implies k\ge 100.
\]
Thus \(|S|\ge 100\).

To keep \(|S|\) minimal, we take exactly one block of size \(100\) attaining \(101\) cousins; that forces \(\#\text{cousins}(B)=101\).

### 5) The remaining factor is \(4040/101=40\), requiring at least 7 more elements
The rest of \(S\) (outside that 100-element block) must contribute exactly \(40=2^3\cdot 5\) cousins.

To get a factor \(5\) in a product of block counts, some block must have cousin count divisible by \(5\), hence \(\ge 5\). But a block of size \(t\) has at most \(t+1\) cousins, so to reach \(\ge 5\) we need \(t\ge 4\). That already uses 4 elements.

If we had only \(6\) elements total to make \(40\), then after using 4 to get the factor \(5\), only 2 elements remain, and those 2 elements can contribute at most \(2\cdot 2=4\) cousins (best case: two isolated elements). So the maximum would be \(5\cdot 4=20<40\). Contradiction.

Hence we need at least \(7\) elements to contribute the factor \(40\).

So overall,
\[
|S|\ge 100+7=107.
\]

\[

\]
(where \(1\) means “in \(S\)”, \(0\) means “not in \(S\)”).

In such a component, if it has \(a\) vertices from \(S\), then it has either \(a\) or \(a+1\) vertices not in \(S\) (because of alternation).

- If it has \(a+1\) non-\(S\) vertices, then exactly **one** non-\(S\) vertex is left unmatched. Choosing which one determines the matching and therefore determines \(T\).

### 1) A graph model
Make a bipartite graph \(G\) whose left vertices are the elements of \(S\), whose right vertices are the integers in \(\mathbb Z\setminus S\) that are adjacent to something in \(S\), and connect \(s\in S\) to \(s\pm1\) if that neighbor is not in \(S\).

Then a cousin \(T\) is exactly a matching in \(G\) that saturates all vertices of \(S\) (each \(s\) matched to one neighbor, and all chosen neighbors distinct). Different matchings give different \(T\)’s, so:

\[
\#\{\text{cousins of }S\}=\#\{\text{matchings saturating }S \text{ in }G\}.
\]

### 2) Structure of \(G\)
Along the integer line, edges in \(G\) occur only across an \(S\)/non-\(S\) boundary. Hence every connected component of \(G\) is a path with vertices alternating between \(S\) and \(\mathbb Z\setminus S\).

In any such component, let it contain \(m\) vertices from \(S\). Then there are only two possibilities:

- **Type A (forced):** the component has the same number of non-\(S\) vertices as \(S\)-vertices (the path starts with an \(S\)-vertex and ends with a non-\(S\)-vertex, or vice versa). Then there is exactly **1** matching saturating \(S\) in this component (everything is forced).

- **Type B (one extra non-\(S\) endpoint):** the component starts and ends with non-\(S\) vertices. Then it has \(m+1\) non-\(S\) vertices and \(m\) \(S\)-vertices. Any matching saturating \(S\) must match all \(m\) \(S\)-vertices, leaving exactly one of the \(m+1\) non-\(S\) vertices unmatched; and the choice of which non-\(S\) vertex is left unmatched determines the matching uniquely.  
  So this component contributes exactly **\(m+1\)** matchings.

Therefore, if the Type B components have \(S\)-sizes \(m_1,m_2,\dots,m_r\), then
\[
\#\{\text{cousins}\}=\prod_{i=1}^r (m_i+1),
\]
(Type A components contribute a factor \(1\) and can be ignored for counting).

### 3) Forcing a factor \(101\)
We are told \(\#\{\text{cousins}\}=4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101\), so \(101\) divides the product \(\prod (m_i+1)\). Since \(101\) is prime, some factor must be a multiple of \(101\). The smallest possible such factor is \(101\) itself, meaning for some Type B component,
\[
m_i+1=101 \quad\Rightarrow\quad m_i=100.
\]
So \(|S|\ge 100\).

### 4) Minimizing the rest
After taking one component with \(m=100\) (contributing factor \(101\)), the remaining factor needed is
\[
\frac{4040}{101}=40.
\]
We must write \(40\) as \(\prod (m_i+1)\) while minimizing \(\sum m_i\). Let \(a_i=m_i+1\ge 2\). Then we want \(\prod a_i=40\) minimizing \(\sum (a_i-1)\).

Splitting a factor always decreases the needed elements: for \(a,b\ge2\),
\[
(ab-1) - \bigl((a-1)+(b-1)\bigr)=(a-1)(b-1)>0,
\]
so using \(ab\) as one factor costs more elements than using \(a\) and \(b\) separately. Hence the minimum occurs when we fully split \(40\) into primes:
\[
40=2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 5.
\]
This corresponds to component sizes
\[
m = 1,1,1,4
\]
(since \(m+1=2\) gives \(m=1\), and \(m+1=5\) gives \(m=4\)), using \(1+1+1+4=7\) additional elements.

Thus the minimum possible size is
\[
|S|_{\min}=100+7=107.
\]

This is exactly the number of matchings that saturate all vertices of \(S\) in the graph on integers where edges connect consecutive integers, with the restriction that matched partners must lie outside \(S\).

### 2) Components multiply
If \(S=S_1\sqcup S_2\) and every element of \(S_1\) is at distance at least \(3\) from every element of \(S_2\), then no integer can be adjacent to both parts. Hence choices of partners for \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are independent, and
\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\#\text{cousins}(S_1)\cdot \#\text{cousins}(S_2).
\]
So the total number of cousins factors over “blocks” separated by gaps \(\ge 3\).

### 3) A key bound for one block
Consider one block \(B\subset S\) (meaning: its elements cannot be split into two parts distance \(\ge 3\) apart). Let \(|B|=m\). Then successive elements of \(B\) differ by \(1\) or \(2\).

Let \(U\) be the set of allowable partners for \(B\), i.e.
\[
U=\{b-1,b+1: b\in B\}\setminus S.
\]
Along the number line, the “allowable edges” (from \(b\in B\) to \(b\pm1\in U\)) form a disjoint union of paths, and since \(B\) is one block, it is a single path. In such a path, either \(|U|=m\) (forced matching, at most \(1\) way) or \(|U|=m+1\), in which case a matching saturating all \(m\) vertices in \(B\) is determined by which one vertex of \(U\) is left unused. Therefore the number of cousin-choices contributed by a block of size \(m\) is at most
\[
m+1.
\]

### 4) Forcing a block of size at least \(100\)
We are told \(\#\text{cousins}(S)=4040=2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101\), so in particular the number of cousins is divisible by \(101\).

By the multiplicativity over blocks, **at least one block must contribute a factor divisible by \(101\)**. If that block has size \(m\), its contribution is \(\le m+1\), hence \(m+1\ge 101\), so
\[
m\ge 100.
\]
Thus \(|S|\ge 100\), and moreover having a block contributing \(202,303,\dots\) would require \(m\ge 201,302,\dots\) which is much worse for minimizing \(|S|\). So the best we can do is a block of size \(100\) contributing exactly \(101\) cousins.

Then the remaining part of \(S\) must contribute
\[
\frac{4040}{101}=40
\]
cousins.

### 5) Minimizing the extra elements needed to get \(40\) cousins
If a set has \(n\) elements, each element has at most two choices (\(\pm1\)), so it has at most \(2^n\) cousins. Hence \(2^5=32<40\), so we need at least \(6\) elements.

But with only \(6\) elements, to get a total of \(40\) cousins we would need a factor \(5\). By the block bound, the smallest block that can contribute a multiple of \(5\) is size \(4\) (contribution \(\le 5\), and \(5\) is the first multiple). If we use \(4\) elements to get factor \(5\), the remaining \(2\) elements can contribute at most \(2^2=4\), so the total would be at most \(5\cdot 4=20\), not \(40\). Therefore **\(6\) elements cannot yield \(40\) cousins**, so we need at least \(7\) elements.

Combining with the required \(100\)-element block,
\[
|S|\ge 100+7=107.

Fix a finite set \(S\subset \mathbb Z\). A set \(T\) is a cousin of \(S\) iff we can assign to each \(s\in S\) a distinct integer \(t\in T\) such that \(|s-t|=1\), and also \(T\cap S=\varnothing\).

Equivalently: for each \(s\in S\), we choose one of the available neighbors \(s-1\) or \(s+1\) that is **not** in \(S\), and all chosen neighbors must be **distinct**. This is exactly a matching that saturates \(S\) in the graph where each \(s\) connects to its available neighbors.

### 2) \(S\) cannot contain three consecutive integers
If \(x,x+1,x+2\in S\), then \(x+1\) has neighbors \(x\) and \(x+2\), both in \(S\), so \(x+1\) has **no** allowable partner in \(T\). Then \(S\) would have **zero** cousins, contradicting that it has \(4040\).

So every run of consecutive integers in \(S\) has length at most \(2\).

### 3) Decompose \(S\) into independent “blocks”
If two elements of \(S\) differ by \(\ge 3\), then their possible partner-neighbors \(\{s\pm1\}\) are disjoint from those of the other element(s), so the choices for \(T\) do not interfere. Thus the total number of cousins factors as a product over **blocks** of \(S\), where a block is a maximal subset of \(S\) whose consecutive elements differ by at most \(2\).

So we analyze one block at a time and multiply.

### 4) Count cousins contributed by one block

#### Block type A: a block containing an adjacent pair
Suppose a block contains \(a,a+1\in S\). Then:
- \(a\) cannot match to \(a+1\), so it is forced to match to \(a-1\).
- \(a+1\) is forced to match to \(a+2\).

Now any other element in the same block must lie within 2 of these, and this forcing propagates outward; each new element has only one available neighbor left once collisions are avoided. Inductively, the entire block has **exactly 1** valid matching, hence contributes a factor \(1\).

So adjacent pairs never help achieve a large prescribed number of cousins with few elements (they add elements but multiply the cousin-count by \(1\)).

#### Block type B: no adjacent pair
Then all gaps inside the block must be exactly \(2\). So the block has the form
\[
\{a,a+2,a+4,\dots,a+2(m-1)\}
\]
with \(m\) elements.

The available neighbor set is
\[
\{a-1,a+1,a+3,\dots,a+2m-1\},
\]
which has \(m+1\) integers. Any valid matching must use \(m\) distinct neighbors, i.e. it leaves **exactly one** of these \(m+1\) unused. Conversely, choosing which neighbor is unused determines a unique matching.

So such a block contributes exactly \(\boxed{m+1}\) cousins.

\[

\]
with the requirements that

- \(T\cap S=\varnothing\) (disjointness), and  
- the values \(s+\varepsilon(s)\) are all distinct (so \(|T|=|S|\)).

## 1) Splitting \(S\) into independent components

Say two integers in \(S\) are *linked* if they differ by \(1\) or \(2\). Let the connected components of \(S\) under these links be \(C_1,\dots,C_r\), with sizes \(|C_i|=m_i\).

If two components are different, then every element of one differs from every element of the other by at least \(3\). Then any chosen images \(s\pm 1\) from different components cannot collide, and also cannot land inside the other component. Hence:

**Independence:** the number of cousins of \(S\) is the product of the numbers of cousins of each component \(C_i\).

So we reduce to counting cousins for one component.

## 2) Counting cousins of one component

Let a component \(C=\{a_1<a_2<cdots<a_m\}\). By definition, each gap \(a_{i+1}-a_i\) is \(1\) or \(2\).

Write \(\varepsilon_i=\varepsilon(a_i)\in\{-1,+1\}\).

### Gap \(1\): \(a_{i+1}=a_i+1\)
Then \(a_i+1\in S\), so \(a_i\) cannot choose \(+1\). Likewise \(a_{i+1}\) cannot choose \(-1\). Thus
\[
\varepsilon_i=-1,\qquad \varepsilon_{i+1}=+1
\]
is forced.

### Gap \(2\): \(a_{i+1}=a_i+2\)
Then the only possible collision is if \(a_i\) chooses \(+1\) and \(a_{i+1}\) chooses \(-1\), because both would map to \(a_i+1\). Thus the pair \((\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_{i+1})=(+1,-1)\) is forbidden.

So along a gap \(2\), we must **not** have \(+1\) followed by \(-1\). If we encode \(-1<+1\), this means the sequence \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_m\) must be **nondecreasing**.

- If the component has **no gap \(1\)** (so all gaps are \(2\)), then any nondecreasing \(\{-1,+1\}\)-sequence is determined by where it switches from \(-1\) to \(+1\). There are \(m+1\) choices (switch after position \(0,1,\dots,m\)).  
  Hence the component has exactly \(m+1\) cousins.

- If the component has **a gap \(1\)**, then at that place we force \(\cdots,-1,+1,\cdots\), which forces the switch point and thus forces the entire nondecreasing sequence. So the component has at most \(1\) cousin (and in fact is impossible if there are two such forced switches).

In all cases, for a component of size \(m\),
\[
\#(\text{cousins of the component}) \le m+1.
\]

## 3) A lower bound for \(|S|\)

Let the component cousin-counts be \(N_1,\dots,N_r\). Then
\[
N_1N_2\cdots N_r = 4040,

and from \(N_i\le m_i+1\) we get
\[
m_i \ge N_i-1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad |S|=\sum_{i=1}^r m_i \ge \sum_{i=1}^r (N_i-1).
\]

Now we minimize \(\sum (N_i-1)\) subject to \(\prod N_i = 4040\) and \(N_i\ge 2\) (we ignore any \(N_i=1\) since it only increases \(|S|\) without changing the product).

Key inequality: if \(N=ab\) with \(a,b\ge 2\), then
\[
(ab-1) - \big((a-1)+(b-1)\big) = (a-1)(b-1)\ge 1,
\]
so splitting a composite factor into smaller factors *decreases* the sum of \((\cdot-1)\). Therefore the minimum occurs when all \(N_i\) are primes, i.e. the prime factorization of \(4040\).

Since
\[
4040 = 2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101,
\]
the minimal possible value is
\[
(2-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)+(5-1)+(101-1)=1+1+1+4+100=107.
\]
So \(|S|\ge 107\).

Because the integer line has no cycles, every connected component of \(G\) is a path. In any component, vertices alternate between \(S\) and \(N\), so if a component contains \(a\) vertices of \(S\), then it contains either \(a\) or \(a+1\) vertices of \(N\) (difference at most \(1\) in a bipartite path).

## 1. Components and the \(k+1\) bound

Two elements of \(S\) can only “interact” (compete for the same neighbor) if they differ by \(2\).  
Indeed, if \(s\) and \(s+2\) are both in \(S\), then they both could try to match to \(s+1\).

This leads to components consisting of arithmetic progressions with difference \(2\) (same parity).  
Consider one such component
\[
C=\{a,a+2,a+4,\dots,a+2(k-1)\}\subseteq S,
\]
with \(k\) elements. The only possible partners for these \(k\) elements lie in the opposite parity set
\[
P=\{a-1,a+1,a+3,\dots,a+2k-1\},
\]
which has \(k+1\) integers.

Each \(a+2i\in C\) can only match to its left or right neighbor in \(P\). Because matches must be distinct, among the \(k+1\) candidates in \(P\), exactly one is left unused. Therefore the number of valid matchings for this component is **at most**
\[
k+1.
\]
Moreover, this maximum \(k+1\) is achieved when none of the integers in \(P\) lie in \(S\) (so all choices are available).

Different components are independent (they use disjoint sets of possible partners), so the total number of cousins is the product of the numbers from each component.

## 2. Forcing a factor of \(101\)

We are told \(S\) has exactly \(4040\) cousins, and
\[
4040 = 2^3\cdot 5 \cdot 101.
\]
Since \(101\) is prime and the total number of cousins is a product over components, **some component’s count must be divisible by \(101\)**.

If a component has \(k\) elements, its count is \(\le k+1\).  
So to have a multiple of \(101\), we need
\[
k+1\ge 101 \quad\Rightarrow\quad k\ge 100.
\]
Thus \(|S|\ge 100\).

To minimize \(|S|\), we should realize the factor \(101\) in the smallest possible way, namely by taking \(k=100\) and achieving exactly \(k+1=101\) cousins from that component.

So we use up \(100\) elements of \(S\) to get the factor \(101\), and the remaining elements must contribute a factor
\[
\frac{4040}{101}=40.
\]

## 3. Minimum size to get \(40\) cousins

Now show any set with \(40\) cousins must have at least \(7\) elements.

## 1) Components multiply, and each component is a “parity path”
In \(\Gamma(S)\), every edge connects an integer to an integer of opposite parity, so every connected component of \(\Gamma(S)\) contains \(S\)-vertices all of the **same parity** (even or odd). Also, if two same-parity elements of \(S\) differ by \(\ge 4\), they share no neighbor, hence lie in different components.

Therefore, \(\Gamma(S)\) is a disjoint union of components, and the number of matchings covering all of \(S\) is the **product** of the numbers of such matchings in each component.

Fix one connected component \(C\). List its \(S\)-vertices in increasing order:
\[
s_1<s_2<\dots < s_r.
\]
Connectivity forces \(s_{i+1}-s_i=2\) for all \(i\) (same parity, and must share the middle neighbor). So \(s_1,s_2,\dots,s_r\) form a consecutive run in steps of 2.

If neither endpoint is “blocked” by an adjacent opposite-parity element of \(S\), then \(C\) has exactly the \(r+1\) neighbor-vertices
\[
s_1-1,\ s_1+1,\ s_2+1,\dots, s_r+1,
\]
and the component looks like an alternating path
\[
N\!-\!S\!-\!N\!-\!S\!-\cdots-\!N
\]
with \(r\) \(S\)-vertices and \(r+1\) \(N\)-vertices.

If an endpoint neighbor is blocked, \(C\) has only \(r\) (or fewer) \(N\)-vertices, which can only **decrease** the number of matchings.

### Claim: A component with \(r\) vertices from \(S\) contributes at most \(r+1\) cousins.
In the “best” case (the alternating path with \(r\) \(S\)’s and \(r+1\) \(N\)’s), any matching covering all \(S\)-vertices must leave exactly one \(N\)-vertex unmatched, and once you choose which \(N\) is unmatched, all edges in the matching are forced along the path. Hence there are exactly \(r+1\) matchings.

In all other cases (missing an endpoint neighbor), there are \(\le 1\) matchings.  
So always:
\[
\text{(component cousin count)}\ \le r+1.
\]
Equivalently, if a component contributes \(c\) cousins, then it must contain at least \(c-1\) elements of \(S\):
\[
r\ge c-1. \tag{1}

Moreover, different connected components of \(G\) contribute independently, so the total number of cousins is the product of the numbers of such matchings over the connected components.

### 2) A connected component contributes either \(1\) or \(k+1\)

\]
Let \(k\) be the number of vertices of \(C\) that lie in \(S\). Along an alternating path, the number of non-\(S\) vertices is either \(k\) (if the path ends in \(S\)) or \(k+1\) (if the path starts and ends outside \(S\)).

Conversely, choosing which of these \(k+1\) non-\(S\) vertices is left unmatched forces the rest of the matching uniquely along the path.

So each component contributes either \(1\) (a “forced” component) or \(k+1\).

Let \(S\subset \mathbb Z\) be finite.  A cousin \(T\) is obtained by pairing each \(s\in S\) with a distinct integer \(t\notin S\) such that \(|s-t|=1\). Equivalently, for each \(s\in S\) we choose either \(s-1\) or \(s+1\), and all chosen values must be distinct and not in \(S\).

---

### 1) Structure forced by having cousins
If \(x,x+1,x+2\in S\), then \(x+1\) can only pair with \(x\) or \(x+2\), both in \(S\), impossible.  
So \(S\) contains no three consecutive integers.

If \(x,x+1\in S\), then \(x\) cannot pair with \(x+1\) (since \(T\cap S=\varnothing\)), so \(x\) is forced to pair with \(x-1\), and similarly \(x+1\) is forced to pair with \(x+2\). This “forcedness” propagates: any element within distance \(2\) of such a consecutive pair also becomes forced, and in fact that whole \(\{1,2\}\)-gap-connected component contributes exactly \(1\) cousin-choice. Including such forced components only increases \(|S|\) without increasing the number of cousins (multiplying by \(1\)), so for the *minimum-size* \(S\) we may assume:

\[
\textbf{No two elements of \(S\) are consecutive.}
\]

Hence any two elements of \(S\) are either \(\ge 3\) apart (independent) or exactly \(2\) apart (the only way choices can interact).

---

### 2) Components are “step-2 chains”
Under “no consecutive elements,” the only interactions happen for elements differing by \(2\). Thus \(S\) splits into independent components separated by gaps \(\ge 3\), and each component must be of the form
\[
\{a,\,a+2,\,a+4,\,\dots,\,a+2(m-1)\}
\]
for some \(m\ge 1\). Call this a step-2 chain of length \(m\).

Because different components are separated by \(\ge 3\), their possible paired elements lie in disjoint parts of \(\mathbb Z\), so:

\[
\#\text{cousins of }S \;=\; \prod (\#\text{cousins of each component}).
\]

---

### 3) Cousins of a step-2 chain: exactly \(m+1\)
Consider a chain \(C=\{a,a+2,\dots,a+2(m-1)\}\). Each element \(a+2i\) chooses \(L=a+2i-1\) or \(R=a+2i+1\). The only possible collision is when two consecutive chain elements choose \(R\) then \(L\), both landing on the same middle integer. So for consecutive elements, the forbidden pattern is:
\[
(R \text{ for } a+2i)\ \text{and}\ (L \text{ for } a+2(i+1)).
\]
Thus once you ever choose \(R\), all later choices must also be \(R\). So valid choice-strings are exactly:
\[
\underbrace{LL\cdots L}_{k}\underbrace{RR\cdots R}_{m-k}\quad (k=0,1,\dots,m),
\]
which are \(m+1\) possibilities. Therefore a chain of length \(m\) has exactly \(m+1\) cousins.

So if \(S\) has chain lengths \(m_1,\dots,m_r\), then
\[
\#\text{cousins}(S)=\prod_{i=1}^r (m_i+1).
\]

---

### 4) Minimize \(|S|=\sum m_i\) given \(\prod(m_i+1)=4040\)
Let \(f_i=m_i+1\ge 2\). Then
\[
\prod f_i = 4040,\qquad |S|=\sum (f_i-1).
\]

Key inequality: if some \(f\) is composite, \(f=ab\) with \(a,b\ge 2\), then replacing \(f\) by \(a\) and \(b\) decreases \(\sum(f_i-1)\) because
\[
(ab-1) - \bigl((a-1)+(b-1)\bigr) = (a-1)(b-1) > 0.
\]
So to minimize \(\sum(f_i-1)\), we should factor \(4040\) completely into primes.

Prime factorization:
\[
4040 = 2^3\cdot 5\cdot 101.
\]
Thus the minimal size is
\[
|S|_{\min} = 3(2-1) + (5-1) + (101-1) = 3 + 4 + 100 = 107.
\]

\]
and \(|S|=100+4+1+1+1=107\).

For fixed relative “which block gets larger numbers”, the best way to minimize all maxima is to give each block a contiguous interval of the smallest available integers (otherwise its own maximum only increases and never helps). Hence it suffices to decide an **order** of the blocks; the maximum of \(A_d\) becomes the endpoint of the latest block among \(\{B_e:e\mid d\}\).
