### 4) Optimal ordering by “push irrelevant large blocks to the end”
Note which \(A_d\) each block can affect:

- \(B_{250}\) appears only in \(A_{250}\). So placing it earlier cannot reduce any \(\max A_d\) (since \(\max A_{250}\) is forced to be \(250\) anyway), but can only increase others by shifting them upward. Hence **\(B_{250}\) should be last**.
- Once \(B_{250}\) is last, all other \(\max A_d\) (for \(d<250\)) depend only on numbers \(\le 150\). The block \(B_{125}\) affects only \(A_{125}\) among the remaining terms, so to avoid shifting many earlier maxima upward, it is optimal to place all blocks needed for \(A_{50}\) before it. Thus we place
  \[
  B_{125}\text{ after }B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50}.
  \]
- Similarly, within \(B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50}\), the block \(B_{50}\) affects only \(A_{50}\), and \(\max A_{50}\) is simply the completion time of the last among these six blocks (which is constant \(50\) if they come before \(B_{125}\)). So \(B_{50}\) should go last among those six to avoid delaying smaller-\(d\) maxima.
- Likewise, \(B_{25}\) affects only \(A_{25}\) (and \(A_{50}\), already constant \(50\)), so it should go after \(B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10}\).
- \(B_{10}\) affects only \(A_{10}\) (and \(A_{50}\)), so it should go after \(B_1,B_2,B_5\).

  \(\max A_1 + \max A_2 + \max A_5\),
  the best order is \(B_1\) then \(B_2\) then \(B_5\) (checked by direct comparison of the 6 permutations).

So an optimal block order is:
\[
B_1,\ B_2,\ B_5,\ B_{10},\ B_{25},\ B_{50},\ B_{125},\ B_{250}.
\]

### 2) “New elements” decomposition and forced sizes
For each positive integer \(n\), define the disjoint “new elements”
\[
D_n \;=\; A_n \setminus \bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}} A_d.
\]
Because of the nesting property, these \(D_n\) are pairwise disjoint, and
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n} D_d,\qquad |A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n} |D_d|.
\]
Since \(|A_n|=n\), Möbius inversion gives
\[
|D_n|=\varphi(n).
\]
Thus for the divisors of \(250\), the sizes are forced:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
n & 1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
|D_n|=\varphi(n) & 1&1&4&4&20&20&100&100
\end{array}
\]
and these \(8\) disjoint blocks together have total size \(250\), i.e. they exactly form \(A_{250}\).

### 3) Reformulating the objective in terms of block maxima
Let
\[
m_n := \max D_n.
\]
Then since \(A_d=\bigcup_{e\mid d} D_e\),
\[
\max A_d = \max_{e\mid d} m_e.
\]

To minimize the maxima, we should label the \(250\) elements of \(A_{250}\) with \(1,2,\dots,250\) (otherwise \(\max A_{250}>250\) unnecessarily). Also, for any \(t\), at most \(t\) elements can have label \(\le t\). Therefore, if we list the blocks \(D_n\) in increasing order of their maxima \(m_n\), then the \(k\)-th block’s maximum must be at least the sum of the sizes of the first \(k\) blocks. Hence, without loss of optimality, we may assume each block occupies a consecutive interval of labels, in some order of the blocks; then each block maximum is exactly a prefix sum.

So the problem becomes: choose an order of the 8 blocks with processing times
\[
(1,1,4,4,20,20,100,100)
\]
to minimize \(\sum_{d\mid 250} \max A_d\), where each \(\max A_d\) is the completion time of the latest block among \(\{D_e:e\mid d\}\).

### 4) Finding the optimal order (forced by “who can finish next”)
Think of each divisor \(d\mid 250\) as a “job” that completes once all blocks \(D_e\) with \(e\mid d\) are placed. The sum of completion times is minimized by always placing a block that allows some job(s) to finish as early as possible; here this forces a unique optimal sequence:

- First must be \(D_1\) (size 1), since no job can finish before \(D_1\).
- Then \(D_2\) (size 1) must come before \(D_5\) (size 4): swapping them shows \(D_2\) first is better because it’s shorter and completes \(A_2\) earlier.
- Next must be \(D_5\), since it is the only remaining block that can complete a new job (\(A_5\)).
- After that, \(D_{10}\) (size 4) must come before \(D_{25}\) (size 20): swapping them shows doing the shorter one first completes \(A_{10}\) earlier and dominates.
- Then \(D_{25}\) must come next (it is the only one that can now complete \(A_{25}\)).
- Next \(D_{50}\) must come before \(D_{125}\): swapping shows \(20\) before \(100\) is better since it completes \(A_{50}\) earlier.
- Finally \(D_{250}\) last, and \(D_{125}\) before it (otherwise \(A_{125}\) is delayed unnecessarily).

Thus the optimal block order is
\[
D_1,\ D_2,\ D_5,\ D_{10},\ D_{25},\ D_{50},\ D_{125},\ D_{250}.
\]

The prefix sums (hence block maxima) are:
\[
1,\ 2,\ 6,\ 10,\ 30,\ 50,\ 150,\ 250.

### 2) Forced “building blocks” \(B_n\) of sizes \(\varphi(n)\)

Define for each \(n\):
\[
B_n \;=\; A_n\setminus\bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}} A_d.
\]
Then the \(B_n\)’s are disjoint, and
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n} B_d \quad\text{(disjoint union)}.
\]
Taking sizes gives
\[
n=|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n} |B_d|.
\]
By Möbius inversion this forces \(|B_n|=\varphi(n)\).

For divisors of \(250=2\cdot 5^3\), the divisors are
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250
\]
and thus the forced block sizes are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
n&1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\\hline
|B_n|=\varphi(n)&1&1&4&4&20&20&100&100
\end{array}
\]

Moreover, for each \(d\mid 250\),
\[
A_d=\bigcup_{n\mid d} B_n,
\]
so
\[
\max A_d = \max_{n\mid d} \bigl(\max B_n\bigr).
\]

Thus the problem becomes: assign distinct positive integers to the disjoint blocks \(B_n\) (with the fixed sizes above) to minimize \(\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d\).

### 3) Scheduling viewpoint (why we may assume contiguous blocks)

List the \(250\) elements of \(A_{250}\) in increasing order of their values; the largest value used is at least \(250\), and we can always take it to be exactly \(250\) by using \(\{1,2,\dots,250\}\) for \(A_{250}\).

Only the **largest** element of each block \(B_n\) matters for all \(\max A_d\). If we sort the blocks by their maximum elements and then “compress” each block to occupy consecutive positions (without changing the relative order of block maxima), no \(\max A_d\) increases. Therefore, the optimum occurs when the blocks are placed as consecutive segments in some order, filled with the smallest available integers.

So we may choose an **order** of the eight blocks; then \(\max B_n\) equals the cumulative total size up to that block.

---

### 4) Determining the optimal order

**(i) \(B_{250}\) must be last.**  
It affects only \(\max A_{250}\), but if it were earlier it would increase \(\max A_d\) for every other \(d\mid 250\). So put \(B_{250}\) last.

**(ii) \(B_{125}\) must be just before \(B_{250}\).**  
\(B_{125}\) affects only \(\max A_{125}\) and \(\max A_{250}\). If any other block were after \(B_{125}\), swapping it to be after that block increases \(\max A_{125}\) by at most the swapped block’s size (at most \(20\)), but decreases at least one of \(\max A_2,\max A_5,\max A_{10},\max A_{25},\max A_{50}\) by \(100\). So \(B_{125}\) should be last among the other seven.

Thus the last two blocks are
\[
B_{125},\;B_{250}.
\]

**(iii) The six blocks in \(A_{50}\) must all occur before \(B_{125}\).**  
Those are \(B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50}\) with total size \(50\). Putting them first gives \(\max A_{50}=50\), which is minimal.

So the first \(50\) integers should be exactly the elements of \(A_{50}\), and then necessarily
\[
\max A_{125} = 50 + 100 = 150
\]
since \(A_{125}\setminus A_{50}\) has \(100\) elements (forced by \(|A_{125}\cap A_{50}|=|A_{25}|=25\)) and none can lie among the first \(50\).

**(iv) To keep \(\max A_{10}\) small, \(B_{25}\) must come after \(B_2,B_5,B_{10}\).**  
If \(B_{25}\) (size \(20\)) is placed before finishing \(B_2,B_5,B_{10}\), then \(\max A_{10}\) jumps by at least \(20\), while \(\max A_{25}\) can drop by at most \(5\) (from \(30\) to \(25\)). Net increase, so \(B_{25}\) must follow all of \(B_2,B_5,B_{10}\).

Also \(B_{50}\) should be after \(B_{25}\) because it affects none of \(A_2,A_5,A_{10},A_{25}\), so placing it earlier only worsens those maxima.

Thus within the first \(50\), the last two blocks are \(B_{25},B_{50}\), and before them are \(B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10}\).

**(v) Optimal order among \(B_2\) and \(B_5\).**  
If \(B_5\) comes before \(B_2\), then \(\max A_5=5\) but \(\max A_2\ge 6\), giving \(\max A_2+\max A_5\ge 11\).  
If \(B_2\) comes before \(B_5\), we can have \(\max A_2=2\) and then \(\max A_5=6\), giving total \(8\), which is smaller. So \(B_2\) must precede \(B_5\). Also \(B_{10}\) should come after \(B_5\) so \(\max A_5\) stays as small as possible.

Therefore the optimal block order is:
\[
B_1,\;B_2,\;B_5,\;B_{10},\;B_{25},\;B_{50},\;B_{125},\;B_{250}.
\]

### 1) Standard structure of such set systems
A classical way to realize
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)\quad(\forall i,j\ge1)
\]
is to take pairwise disjoint finite sets \(B_n\) with
\[
|B_n|=\varphi(n)
\]
and define
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n} B_d.
\]
Then
\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)} B_d
\]
(disjoint union), so
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\sum_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)} |B_d|
=\sum_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(d)=\gcd(i,j),
\]
using the identity \(\sum_{d\mid m}\varphi(d)=m\). Also \(|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\).

So we may assume wlog the system comes from such disjoint blocks \(B_n\).

### 2) Only divisors of \(250\) matter
We need \(\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d\). For \(d\mid 250\), the set \(A_d\) only uses blocks \(B_e\) with \(e\mid d\), hence only \(e\mid 250\) are relevant.

Divisors of \(250=2\cdot 5^3\) are:
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250.
\]
Their block sizes are \(|B_d|=\varphi(d)\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
\varphi(d)&1&1&4&4&20&20&100&100
\end{array}
\]
These sum to \(250\), so \(A_{250}\) is exactly the union of these \(250\) elements.

Since \(A_{250}\) has \(250\) distinct positive integers, \(\max A_{250}\ge 250\), and we can achieve equality by using the labels \(1,2,\dots,250\). Hence
\[
\min \max A_{250}=250.
\]

### 3) A monotonicity exchange: we can assume “divisibility implies smaller max”
If \(a\mid b\), then every set \(A_d\) that contains \(B_b\) also contains \(B_a\). If some element of \(B_a\) is labeled larger than some element of \(B_b\), swapping those labels cannot increase any \(\max A_d\) (the larger label moves to a block that appears in fewer relevant \(A_d\)’s). Repeating, we may assume:
\[
a\mid b \implies \max B_a \le \max B_b.
\]
Then for each divisor \(d\mid 250\), every \(B_e\) with \(e\mid d\) has \(\max B_e\le \max B_d\), so
\[
\max A_d=\max B_d.
\]
Therefore the target becomes minimizing
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} \max B_d.
\]

### 4) Rephrase as a precedence-constrained scheduling problem
Assign the labels \(1,2,\dots,250\) to the \(250\) elements in the blocks \(B_d\) for \(d\mid 250\). Let
\[
m_d:=\max B_d.
\]
The condition \(a\mid b\Rightarrow m_a\le m_b\) acts like a precedence constraint.

Because each \(B_d\) needs \(\varphi(d)\) distinct labels \(\le m_d\), the optimal situation is to place each block in contiguous chunks in increasing label order; then \(m_d\) is exactly the “completion time” of job \(d\) in a schedule.

So we have 8 jobs with processing times \(p_d=\varphi(d)\) and precedence \(a\mid b\Rightarrow a\) must be scheduled before \(b\), and we want to minimize the sum of completion times \(\sum m_d\).

Jobs (with \(p\)) and required precedence:
- \(1(1)\) first.
- After \(1\): available \(2(1)\), \(5(4)\).
- \(10(4)\) after \(2,5\).
- \(25(20)\) after \(5\).
- \(50(20)\) after \(10,25,2\).
- \(125(100)\) after \(25,5\).
- \(250(100)\) after everything.

We can now check all possible branches (few) to find the minimum total completion time.

### 5) Compute the optimal order and sum
**Case A:** start \(1,2,5\) (forced if we pick \(2\) second).
Time/completions:
- \(1\): \(C_1=1\)
- \(2\): \(C_2=2\)
- \(5\): \(C_5=6\)

Now available: \(10(4)\) and \(25(20)\).

**A1:** do \(10\) then \(25\):
- \(10\): \(C_{10}=10\)
- \(25\): \(C_{25}=30\)

Now available: \(50(20)\), \(125(100)\). Compare orders:
- \(50\) then \(125\): \(C_{50}=50,\ C_{125}=150\)
- \(125\) then \(50\): \(C_{125}=130,\ C_{50}=150\) (worse because \(50\) gets delayed a lot)

So choose \(50\) then \(125\), then \(250\):
- \(250\): \(C_{250}=250\)

Sum:
\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

**A2:** do \(25\) then \(10\) gives \(C_{25}=26,\ C_{10}=30\), and the best completion-sum in that branch is \(515>499\).

So Case A minimum is \(499\).

**Case B:** start \(1,5\).
At time 5, you may do \(2\) next or \(25\) next. One checks:
- If \(1,5,2,\dots\), best total is \(502\).
- If \(1,5,25,2,\dots\), best total is \(537\).

So Case B is worse than \(499\).

Hence the global minimum is **\(499\)**.

Taking \(i=j\) gives
\[
|A_i|=|A_i\cap A_i|=\gcd(i,i)=i.
\]
So each \(A_i\) has exactly \(i\) elements.

If \(d\mid n\), then \(\gcd(d,n)=d\), hence
\[
|A_d\cap A_n|=d=|A_d|.
\]
So \(A_d\subseteq A_n\). In particular, for any \(i,j\),
\[
A_{\gcd(i,j)}\subseteq A_i\cap A_j
\]
and both sides have size \(\gcd(i,j)\), so
\[
A_i\cap A_j = A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|A_i\cup A_j|=|A_i|+|A_j|-|A_i\cap A_j| = i+j-\gcd(i,j).
\]

### 2) A key inequality involving maxima

Let \(M_k=\max A_k\). Then \(A_k\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,M_k\}\), so \(|A_k|\le M_k\), i.e.
\[
M_k\ge k.
\]
Also, if \(T=\max(M_i,M_j)\), then \(A_i\cup A_j\subseteq\{1,\dots,T\}\), hence
\[
T\ge |A_i\cup A_j| = i+j-\gcd(i,j).
\]
So we always have
\[
\max(M_i,M_j)\ \ge\ i+j-\gcd(i,j). \tag{*}
\]

### 1) A standard model for such sets

Let \(\{B_n\}_{n\ge 1}\) be pairwise disjoint finite sets with  
\[
|B_n|=\varphi(n)\quad(\text{Euler totient}).
\]
Define
\[
A_m=\bigcup_{d\mid m} B_d.
\]
Then for any \(i,j\),
\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{d\mid i,\ d\mid j} B_d=\bigcup_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)} B_d,
\]
so
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\sum_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)} |B_d|
=\sum_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(d)=\gcd(i,j),
\]
using the identity \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\).  
So this construction satisfies the condition.

For \(d\mid 250\), the set \(A_d\) only uses blocks \(B_t\) with \(t\mid 250\). The total size of those blocks is
\[
\sum_{t\mid 250}\varphi(t)=250,
\]
so we may assign **exactly** the integers \(1,2,\dots,250\) to the elements in \(\bigcup_{t\mid 250} B_t\).  
All other \(B_n\) (with \(n\nmid 250\)) can use integers \(>250\), which does not affect any \(\max A_d\) for \(d\mid 250\).

Thus the problem reduces to: assign the integers \(1,\dots,250\) to the blocks \(B_t\) for \(t\mid 250\) (disjointly) to minimize \(\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d\).

### 3) Choosing the optimal block order

- **\(B_1\) must be first**, else \(\max A_1>1\) and the sum increases.
- **\(B_{250}\)** appears only in \(A_{250}\), whose maximum is fixed at \(250\). Putting \(B_{250}\) anywhere but last would delay (increase) \(\max A_2,\max A_5,\max A_{10},\max A_{25},\max A_{50},\max A_{125}\) with no benefit. Hence \(B_{250}\) should be last among the \(t\mid 250\) blocks.

Now consider \(A_{50}\): it uses exactly the blocks
\[
B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50}
\]
whose total size is \(50\). Therefore \(\max A_{50}\ge 50\), and to achieve \(\max A_{50}=50\) we must place **all** these blocks before any of \(B_{125},B_{250}\). Any insertion of \(B_{125}\) or \(B_{250}\) before finishing these would force \(\max A_{50}\ge 150\) or \(\ge 250\), far worse.

Similarly, \(A_{125}\) uses blocks \(B_1,B_5,B_{25},B_{125}\) of total size \(125\), so \(\max A_{125}\ge 125\); but we will already be placing \(B_2,B_{10},B_{50}\) before \(B_{125}\) (to keep \(A_{50}\) small), inevitably pushing \(\max A_{125}\) above \(125\).

Thus the optimal global structure is:
\[
B_1,\ \ (\text{some order of }B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50}),\ \ B_{125},\ \ B_{250}.
\]
Moreover, since \(B_{50}\) is not needed for \(A_2,A_5,A_{10},A_{25},A_{125}\), placing it before completing those only delays them, so it should come after \(B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25}\).

So we must optimize the order of the four blocks
\[
B_2(1),\ B_5(4),\ B_{10}(4),\ B_{25}(20)
\]
before \(B_{50}\).

**Key point:** If \(B_{25}\) is not last among these four, then one of \(B_2,B_5,B_{10}\) is last, so \(\max A_{10}\) becomes the time after all four blocks, i.e. \(30\) instead of \(10\). That alone increases the sum by \(20\), while the best possible improvement to \(\max A_{25}\) from moving \(B_{25}\) earlier is at most \(5\). Hence \(B_{25}\) must be last among these four.

With \(B_{25}\) last, \(\max A_{10}\) is fixed at \(10\), and we minimize \(\max A_2+\max A_5\) by placing \(B_2\) before \(B_5\) (since \(1\) is smaller than \(4\)).

Thus the optimal order is:
\[
B_1,\ B_2,\ B_5,\ B_{10},\ B_{25},\ B_{50},\ B_{125},\ B_{250}.
\]

\[

### 2) Forced “totient-layer” decomposition

Define for each \(n\ge 1\):
\[

These are the “new” elements appearing at level \(n\).

**Claim 1: The sets \(B_n\) are pairwise disjoint.**  
If \(x\in B_m\cap B_n\), then \(x\in A_m\cap A_n=A_{\gcd(m,n)}\). But \(\gcd(m,n)<m\) or \(<n\) unless \(m=n\); this would place \(x\) in a proper divisor set of \(A_m\) contradicting \(x\in B_m\). Hence \(m=n\).

\[
A_n=\bigsqcup_{d\mid n} B_d

(disjoint union).  
Indeed, every element of \(A_n\) lies in some minimal \(A_d\) (under divisibility), and then lies in \(B_d\); conversely each \(B_d\subseteq A_n\) when \(d\mid n\).

Taking sizes:
\[
n=|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}|B_d|.
\]
By Möbius inversion this forces
\[
|B_n|=\varphi(n)\quad\text{for all }n.
\]

So the sizes of the layers \(B_d\) are **uniquely determined**.

### 2) A useful lemma (pigeonhole bound from intersection size)

Let finite sets \(X,Y\subseteq \{1,2,\dots\}\) with \(|X|=a,\ |Y|=b,\ |X\cap Y|=c\).  
If \(\max X\le \max Y = M\), then \(X\subseteq \{1,\dots,M\}\) uses \(a\) distinct numbers \(\le M\).  
The set \(Y\setminus X\) has size \(b-c\) and must also lie in \(\{1,\dots,M\}\) but outside \(X\), so
\[
M-a \ge b-c \quad\Rightarrow\quad M\ge a+b-c.
\]
So, whenever \(\max X\le \max Y\), we have
\[
\max Y \ge |X|+|Y|-|X\cap Y|.
\]

### 2) Reducing to an ordering / “maximum-per-atom” problem
Let
\[
m_e=\max B_e \qquad (e\mid 250).

Then for each divisor \(d\mid 250\),
\[
\max A_d=\max_{e\mid d} m_e,
\]
since \(A_d\) is a union of disjoint \(B_e\).

Feasibility constraint (pigeonhole/Hall): if we look at all atoms whose maximum is \(\le t\), all their elements must lie in \(\{1,\dots,t\}\). Thus for every \(t\),
\[
\sum_{e:\,m_e\le t} |B_e|\;\le\; t.
\]
Equivalently, if we sort atoms by increasing \(m_e\), the \(k\)-th smallest maximum is at least the cumulative size of the first \(k\) atoms. So in an optimum we may take these inequalities tight: the best way is to order the atoms and assign them consecutive integers so each atom’s maximum equals the running cumulative total.

Thus we only need to find the best order of the eight atoms \(B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50},B_{125},B_{250}\) (with sizes \(1,1,4,4,20,20,100,100\)).

### 3) Determining the optimal order
- \(B_1\) must come first (otherwise \(\max A_1=m_1>1\), and since \(A_1\subseteq A_d\) for all \(d\), all maxima weakly increase).
- \(B_{250}\) should come last: it only affects \(\max A_{250}\), which is fixed at \(250\) anyway, but placing it earlier would shift many other atoms’ maxima upward by \(100\).

Now consider the remaining atoms and which maxima they influence:
- \(A_2\) depends on \(B_2\) (and \(B_1\)), so to keep \(\max A_2\) minimal we must place \(B_2\) immediately after \(B_1\). Otherwise at least \(4\) (or more) extra elements would be forced before finishing \(B_2\), pushing \(\max A_2\) up.
- Similarly, \(A_5\) depends on \(B_5\), and after fixing \(B_1,B_2\) first, the smallest possible \(\max A_5\) occurs by placing \(B_5\) next.
- \(A_{10}\) depends on \(B_{10}\) in addition to \(B_2,B_5\); to keep \(\max A_{10}\) minimal, \(B_{10}\) must come next.
- The same logic continues: \(A_{25}\) forces \(B_{25}\) next, \(A_{50}\) forces \(B_{50}\) before \(B_{125}\), and finally \(B_{125}\).

So the optimal order is
\[
B_1,\;B_2,\;B_5,\;B_{10},\;B_{25},\;B_{50},\;B_{125},\;B_{250}.

With tight assignment, the atom maxima are the cumulative sums:
\[
m_1=1,\ m_2=2,\ m_5=6,\ m_{10}=10,\ m_{25}=30,\ m_{50}=50,\ m_{125}=150,\ m_{250}=250.

Therefore
\[
(\max A_1,\max A_2,\max A_5,\max A_{10},\max A_{25},\max A_{50},\max A_{125},\max A_{250})
=(1,2,6,10,30,50,150,250)
\]
and the sum is
\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

First note that for every \(n\),
\[

Also, if \(d\mid n\), then \(\gcd(d,n)=d\), so
\[
|A_d\cap A_n|=d=|A_d|.

Hence \(A_d\subseteq A_n\). In particular, for all \(i,j\),
\[
A_{\gcd(i,j)}\subseteq A_i\cap A_j

and the two sets have the same size:

|A_{\gcd(i,j)}|=\gcd(i,j)=|A_i\cap A_j|,

### 2) Decomposition into “primitive” disjoint blocks \(S_m\)

For any element \(x\) that appears in at least one set, define its *minimal index*
\[
m(x)=\min\{n:\ x\in A_n\}.
\]
Using (1): if \(x\in A_i\) and \(x\in A_j\), then \(x\in A_{\gcd(i,j)}\). This forces the set of indices containing \(x\) to be closed under gcd, and with the divisibility nesting \(A_d\subseteq A_n\) for \(d\mid n\), one gets:
\[
x\in A_n \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m(x)\mid n.
\]
So each element belongs to *exactly* those \(A_n\) whose indices are multiples of its minimal index.

Define
\[
S_m=\{x:\ m(x)=m\}.
\]
Then the \(S_m\) are disjoint, and for every \(n\),
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{m\mid n} S_m. \tag{2}
\]
Taking sizes and using \(|A_n|=n\),
\[
n=\sum_{m\mid n} |S_m|.
\]
By Möbius inversion this forces
\[
|S_n|=\varphi(n)\quad\text{for all }n. \tag{3}
\]

So the structure (2)–(3) is not just a construction; it is **forced**.

### 2) A key lemma about maxima of two sets
**Lemma.** If \(S,T\) are finite sets of positive integers with
\[
|S|=s,\quad |T|=t,\quad |S\cap T|=u,
\]
then
\[
\max S+\max T \;\ge\; (s+t-u)+\min(s,t).
\]

**Proof.** Let \(M=\max(S\cup T)=\max(\max S,\max T)\). Since \(|S\cup T|=s+t-u\), any set of that size has maximum at least its size, so
\[
M\ge s+t-u.
\]
Let \(m=\min(\max S,\max T)\). The set achieving this smaller maximum has at least \(\min(s,t)\) elements, hence \(m\ge \min(s,t)\).
Therefore,
\[
\max S+\max T = M+m \ge (s+t-u)+\min(s,t).
\]
\(\square\)

\[
A_i\cap A_j = A_{\gcd(i,j)}.

This forces a “block decomposition”: define, for each \(n\),
\[
B_n := A_n \setminus \bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}} A_d.
\]
Then the \(B_n\)’s are pairwise disjoint, and
\[
A_n=\bigsqcup_{d\mid n} B_d.
\]
Taking sizes:
\[
n=|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}|B_d|.
\]
By Möbius inversion, this forces \(|B_n|=\varphi(n)\) (since \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\)).

\[
|A_m\cup A_n|\le \max(x_m,x_n).

But
\[
|A_m\cup A_n|=|A_m|+|A_n|-|A_m\cap A_n|
= m+n-\gcd(m,n).
\]

\[

\[

\]
so \(\max(x_{10},x_{25})\ge 30\). With \(x_{10}\ge 10\), \(x_{25}\ge 25\), the minimum of \(x_{10}+x_{25}\) is achieved by \((10,30)\), hence

\[
|A_{50}\cup A_{125}|=50+125-\gcd(50,125)=175-25=150

\[

\ge 1+8+40+200+250=499.

From \(|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)\), plugging \(i=j=n\) gives
\[
|A_n|=|A_n\cap A_n|=\gcd(n,n)=n.
\]
Also, if \(i\mid j\), then \(\gcd(i,j)=i\), so
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=|A_i| \implies A_i\subseteq A_j.
\]
In particular, for divisors of \(250\), we have many forced inclusions (e.g. \(A_{25}\subseteq A_{250}\), etc.).

A standard (and optimal-for-maxima) way to realize all these intersection sizes is to decompose into disjoint “atoms” \(B_d\) (for \(d\mid 250\)) such that
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n} B_d,\qquad |B_d|=\varphi(d),
\]
because then
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\sum_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)} |B_d|=\sum_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(d)=\gcd(i,j).
\]

For \(250=2\cdot 5^3\), its positive divisors are
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250,
\]
and Euler \(\varphi\) values are
\[
\varphi(1)=1,\ \varphi(2)=1,\ \varphi(5)=4,\ \varphi(10)=4,\ \varphi(25)=20,\ \varphi(50)=20,\ \varphi(125)=100,\ \varphi(250)=100.
\]

### 2) Turning the problem into an ordering problem

Since \(|A_{250}|=250\), we always have \(\max A_{250}\ge 250\). To minimize the sum, we must achieve equality, so we may (and do) label the \(250\) elements of \(A_{250}\) as \(\{1,2,\dots,250\}\).

Now each \(A_d\) is a union of some blocks \(B_k\), so \(\max A_d\) is the largest label among the blocks included in \(A_d\), i.e. the endpoint of the *latest* block (in label order) among those \(k\mid d\).

Interleaving elements of different blocks cannot reduce any \(\max A_d\), so we may assume each block occupies a consecutive interval of labels; then the only decision is the **order** of the blocks.

---

### 3) Determining the optimal block order (exchange arguments)

Write the blocks with sizes:
\[
B_1(1),\ B_2(1),\ B_5(4),\ B_{10}(4),\ B_{25}(20),\ B_{50}(20),\ B_{125}(100),\ B_{250}(100).
\]

**(i) \(B_1\) must be first.** Since \(A_1=B_1\), we need \(\max A_1\ge 1\) and equality forces its element to be label \(1\).

**(ii) \(B_{250}\) must be last.** It appears only in \(A_{250}\), and \(\max A_{250}=250\) is fixed anyway; placing \(B_{250}\) earlier can only push other blocks’ labels higher, increasing some other \(\max A_d\).

Now consider adjacent swaps; later blocks’ endpoints don’t change (same total length before them), so only the affected \(\max A_d\)’s matter.

- **\(B_2\) before \(B_5\):** If \(B_5\) precedes \(B_2\), then \(\max A_2\) increases by \(4\) (since \(A_2\) needs \(B_2\)), while \(\max A_5\) decreases by only \(1\). Net increase \(\ge 3\). So \(B_2\prec B_5\).

- **\(B_5\) before \(B_{10}\):** Swapping to \(B_{10}\prec B_5\) forces \(\max A_5\) to increase by \(4\), while \(\max A_{10}\) does not decrease (it still needs both). So \(B_5\prec B_{10}\).

- **\(B_{10}\) before \(B_{25}\):** If \(B_{25}\prec B_{10}\), then \(\max A_{10}\) increases by \(20\), while \(\max A_{25}\) can decrease by at most \(4\). Net increase \(\ge 16\). So \(B_{10}\prec B_{25}\).

- **\(B_{25}\) before \(B_{50}\):** If \(B_{50}\prec B_{25}\), \(\max A_{25}\) increases by \(20\), while \(\max A_{50}\) does not decrease (it needs both). So \(B_{25}\prec B_{50}\).

- **\(B_{50}\) before \(B_{125}\):** If \(B_{125}\prec B_{50}\), then \(\max A_{50}\) increases by \(100\) (since \(A_{50}\) needs \(B_{50}\) but not \(B_{125}\)), while \(\max A_{125}\) decreases by only \(20\). Net increase \(\ge 80\). So \(B_{50}\prec B_{125}\).

Combining all forced comparisons, the optimal order is uniquely:
\[
B_1,\ B_2,\ B_5,\ B_{10},\ B_{25},\ B_{50},\ B_{125},\ B_{250}.
\]

### 1) Immediate structure forced by the condition

Given \(|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)\) for all \(i,j\):

- Setting \(i=j\) gives \(|A_i|=\gcd(i,i)=i\).
- If \(j\mid i\), then \(|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)=j=|A_j|\), so \(A_j\subseteq A_i\).
- For general \(i,j\), let \(g=\gcd(i,j)\). Since \(g\mid i\) and \(g\mid j\), we have \(A_g\subseteq A_i\cap A_j\). But
  \[
  |A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)=g=|A_g|,
  \]
  hence
  \[
  A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
  \]

So membership is “upward-closed” in divisibility.

### 2) Decomposition into disjoint “minimal-index” blocks

For an element \(x\), let \(m(x)\) be the smallest index with \(x\in A_{m(x)}\). From the intersection rule above, one checks:

- \(x\in A_n\) **iff** \(m(x)\mid n\).

Therefore, for each \(m\ge1\), define the disjoint block
\[
B_m=\{x:\ m(x)=m\}.
\]
Then
\[
A_n=\bigsqcup_{m\mid n} B_m
\]
(disjoint union), so
\[
n=|A_n|=\sum_{m\mid n} |B_m|.
\]
By Möbius inversion (or the classic identity \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\)), this forces
\[
|B_n|=\varphi(n).
\]

So for each divisor \(d\mid 250\), the block \(B_d\) has fixed size \(\varphi(d)\), and \(A_d\) is the union of the blocks \(B_m\) with \(m\mid d\).

For \(250=2\cdot 5^3\), the divisors are
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250
\]
and the block sizes are:
\[
\varphi(1)=1,\ \varphi(2)=1,\ \varphi(5)=4,\ \varphi(10)=4,\ \varphi(25)=20,\ \varphi(50)=20,\ \varphi(125)=100,\ \varphi(250)=100.
\]
These sum to \(250\), so \(A_{250}\) uses exactly \(250\) distinct integers.

### 3) WLOG make the relevant labels be \(1,2,\dots,250\)

Since \(A_{250}\) has size \(250\), \(\max A_{250}\ge 250\). To minimize the sum, we may (and do) take
\[
A_{250}=\{1,2,\dots,250\},
\]
so \(\max A_{250}=250\), and the eight blocks \(B_d\) (for \(d\mid 250\)) partition \(\{1,\dots,250\}\). Any other blocks \(B_n\) with \(n\nmid 250\) can be assigned integers \(>250\) and won’t affect the requested sum.

To minimize maxima of various unions, it is optimal to assign each block a consecutive interval of integers in some order (otherwise you can “compress” a block downward without hurting disjointness and never increase any \(\max A_d\)). Thus we only need choose an order of the 8 blocks along \(1,2,\dots,250\).

---

### 4) Choosing the optimal order of blocks

Think of placing the blocks in a sequence; the end position of a block is the largest integer in it.

Crucial observation: whenever a divisor-set \(A_d\) becomes fully “available” (i.e. all blocks \(B_m\) with \(m\mid d\) have been placed), its maximum is the current position. So to keep the total sum small, we want to complete smaller \(A_d\)’s as early as possible, especially before placing very large blocks.

This forces the following order:

- \(B_1\) must be first (otherwise \(\max A_1\) is larger and, since \(A_1\subseteq A_d\) for all \(d\mid 250\), it pushes up *all* maxima).
- Next \(B_2\) should be as early as possible to complete \(A_2\).
- Next \(B_5\) should be as early as possible to complete \(A_5\).
- Next \(B_{10}\) should be before \(B_{25}\): after placing \(B_1,B_2,B_5\), the set \(A_{10}\) is missing only \(B_{10}\) (size \(4\)), while \(B_{25}\) (size \(20\)) would not complete \(A_{10}\). Placing \(B_{25}\) first would keep \(A_{10}\) unfinished for an extra \(20\) steps, worsening the sum.
- Similarly, after \(B_{25}\), we place \(B_{50}\) (to complete \(A_{50}\)), then \(B_{125}\), then \(B_{250}\).

So the optimal order is
\[
B_1,\ B_2,\ B_5,\ B_{10},\ B_{25},\ B_{50},\ B_{125},\ B_{250}.
\]

Assign consecutive integers to these blocks in that order:

- \(B_2=\{2\}\)  (max \(2\))
- \(B_5=\{3,4,5,6\}\)  (max \(6\))
- \(B_{10}=\{7,8,9,10\}\)  (max \(10\))
- \(B_{25}=\{11,12,\dots,30\}\)  (max \(30\))
- \(B_{50}=\{31,32,\dots,50\}\)  (max \(50\))
- \(B_{125}=\{51,52,\dots,150\}\)  (max \(150\))
- \(B_{250}=\{151,152,\dots,250\}\)  (max \(250\))

Then for each divisor \(d\mid 250\), \(A_d\) is the union of \(B_m\) for \(m\mid d\), so its maximum is the largest maximum among those blocks:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max A_1&=1\\
\max A_2&=2\\
\max A_5&=6\\
\max A_{10}&=10\\
\max A_{25}&=30\\
\max A_{50}&=50\\
\max A_{125}&=150\\
\max A_{250}&=250.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} \max A_d = 1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

This value is achievable by the construction above and is minimal by the forced optimal ordering argument.

\[
\boxed{499}

### 2) A universal lower bound via a lemma on two sets

**Lemma.** If \(X,Y\) are finite sets of positive integers with
\[
|X|=a,\quad |Y|=b,\quad |X\cap Y|=c,
\]
then
\[
\max X+\max Y\ \ge\ 2a+b-c.
\]

**Proof.** Let \(m_X=\max X\), \(m_Y=\max Y\).

- If \(m_X\le m_Y\), then \(X\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,m_Y\}\), so there are \(m_Y-a\) integers \(\le m_Y\) not in \(X\). But \(Y\) needs \(b-c\) elements outside \(X\), all \(\le m_Y\), so \(m_Y-a\ge b-c\), i.e. \(m_Y\ge a+b-c\). Hence
  \[
  m_X+m_Y\ge a+(a+b-c)=2a+b-c.
  \]
- If \(m_X>m_Y\), then at least \(c\) elements of \(X\) are \(\le m_Y\) (the intersection), so \(X\) has \(a-c\) elements \(>m_Y\). The smallest possible maximum then is \(m_X\ge m_Y+(a-c)\), giving
  \[
  m_X+m_Y\ge 2m_Y+(a-c)\ge 2b+(a-c)\ge 2a+b-c
  \]
  since \(b\ge a\) in our applications below.

Thus always \(m_X+m_Y\ge 2a+b-c\). \(\square\)

Now apply this to three disjoint pairs of divisors of \(250\):

1. For \((A_2,A_5)\): \(|A_2|=2\), \(|A_5|=5\), \(|A_2\cap A_5|=\gcd(2,5)=1\).
   \[
   \max A_2+\max A_5\ge 2\cdot 2+5-1=8.
   \]

2. For \((A_{10},A_{25})\): \(|A_{10}|=10\), \(|A_{25}|=25\), \(|A_{10}\cap A_{25}|=\gcd(10,25)=5\).
   \[
   \max A_{10}+\max A_{25}\ge 2\cdot 10+25-5=40.
   \]

3. For \((A_{50},A_{125})\): \(|A_{50}|=50\), \(|A_{125}|=125\), \(|A_{50}\cap A_{125}|=\gcd(50,125)=25\).
   \[
   \max A_{50}+\max A_{125}\ge 2\cdot 50+125-25=200.
   \]

Also trivially, since \(|A_1|=1\) and \(|A_{250}|=250\),
\[
\max A_1\ge 1,\qquad \max A_{250}\ge 250.
\]

Therefore
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
=(\max A_1)+(\max A_2+\max A_5)+(\max A_{10}+\max A_{25})+(\max A_{50}+\max A_{125})+(\max A_{250})
\]
\[
\ge 1+8+40+200+250=499.
\]

So **the minimum is at least \(499\)**.

Let the sequence of top faces rolled be \((f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4,f_5,f_6)\), each uniformly random from \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\).

Define event \(E\): all even-numbered stickers (2,4,6) are visible at the end.

### 1) Count sequences in \(E\)
Let \(a=f_2\) (where sticker 2 is placed) and \(b=f_4\) (where sticker 4 is placed).

For sticker 2 to remain visible, none of rolls 3–6 can land on face \(a\):
- \(f_3,f_4,f_5,f_6 \neq a\).

For sticker 4 to remain visible, rolls 5–6 cannot land on face \(b\):
- \(f_5,f_6 \neq b\).

Also, for sticker 6 to be visible while keeping 2 and 4 visible, \(f_6\neq a,b\) (already included above).

Counting choices:
- \(f_1\): \(6\) choices
- \(f_2=a\): \(6\) choices
- \(f_3\neq a\): \(5\) choices
- \(f_4\neq a\): \(5\) choices
- \(f_5\neq a,b\): \(4\) choices
- \(f_6\neq a,b\): \(4\) choices

So
\[
|E| = 6\cdot 6\cdot 5\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 4 = 14400.
\]

### 2) Count sequences in \(B\cap E\)
Let event \(B\) be: exactly one face is blank at the end.

A face is blank iff it is never rolled, so “exactly one face blank” means exactly \(5\) distinct faces appear among the 6 rolls. Thus among \((f_1,\dots,f_6)\) there must be **exactly one repeated face**, appearing **exactly twice**, and all other faces distinct.

Under \(E\), note:
- \(f_2=a\) cannot equal \(f_3,f_4,f_5,f_6\), so \(a\) can only possibly match \(f_1\).
- \(f_4=b\) cannot equal \(f_5,f_6\), but could match \(f_1\) or \(f_3\).
- \(f_5,f_6\) both lie in the 4-face set \(R=\{1,\dots,6\}\setminus\{a,b\}\).

- \(x_5\) and \(x_6\) may equal each other, and may equal \(x_1\) or \(x_3\) if not forbidden.

The allowed equal pairs are:
\[
(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(1,5),(1,6),(3,4),(3,5),(3,6),(5,6)
\]
which is 9 pairs.

---

## 4) Count sequences for one such pair
Example for pair \((1,2)\): set \(x_1=x_2=a\).
Then \(x_3,x_4,x_5,x_6\) must all be distinct from each other and from \(a\), and the constraints of \(E\) are automatically satisfied.

Count:
\[
6\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2 = 720.
\]
(Choose \(a\), then choose 4 distinct remaining faces for \(x_3,x_4,x_5,x_6\).)

A similar count works for each of the 9 allowed pairs; in each case we end up choosing 5 distinct faces (one repeated once), giving again \(720\) sequences per pair.

Hence
\[
N_{B\cap E} = 9\cdot 720 = 6480.
\]

---

## 5) Conditional probability
\[
p=\frac{N_{B\cap E}}{N_E}=\frac{6480}{14400}=\frac{9}{20}.
\]
So \(m=9\), \(n=20\), and \(m+n=29\).

\[
\boxed{29}
\]

Label the six physical faces of the die by \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). Each roll is then an independent uniform choice of one of these faces to land on top.

Let \(t_k\) be the top face on the \(k\)-th roll (when sticker \(k\) is placed). Then the final visible sticker on any face is the largest index \(k\) such that \(t_k\) equals that face.

### 1) Count the event \(E\): all even stickers \(2,4,6\) are visible
- Sticker \(2\) is visible \(\iff\) no later sticker lands on face \(t_2\), i.e. \(t_3,t_4,t_5,t_6 \neq t_2\).
- Sticker \(4\) is visible \(\iff\) \(t_5,t_6 \neq t_4\).
- Sticker \(6\) is always visible (nothing comes after it).

So \(E\) is exactly the set of sequences \((t_1,\dots,t_6)\) such that
\[
t_3,t_4,t_5,t_6 \neq t_2,\quad \text{and}\quad t_5,t_6 \neq t_4.
\]

Count sequences satisfying \(E\):
- \(t_2\): \(6\) choices.
- \(t_3\): \(5\) choices (not \(t_2\)).
- \(t_4\): \(5\) choices (not \(t_2\)).
- \(t_5\): \(4\) choices (not \(t_2\) or \(t_4\)).
- \(t_6\): \(4\) choices (not \(t_2\) or \(t_4\)).
- \(t_1\): \(6\) choices (no restriction).

Thus
\[
|E| = 6\cdot 5\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 4\cdot 6 = 14400.
\]

### 2) Interpret “exactly one face left blank”
A face is blank at the end iff it was never the top face on any roll. So “exactly one face blank” means exactly \(5\) distinct faces appear among \(t_1,\dots,t_6\). Equivalently: among the 6 rolls, exactly one face is repeated (appears twice) and the other four used faces appear once.

Call this event \(B\).

### 3) Count \(B\cap E\)
Under \(B\), there is exactly one repeated pair of positions \((i,j)\) with \(t_i=t_j\), and all other \(t_k\) are distinct from each other and from that repeated value.

But under \(E\), certain equalities are forbidden:
- \(t_2\) cannot equal \(t_3,t_4,t_5,t_6\): forbidden pairs \((2,3),(2,4),(2,5),(2,6)\) (4 pairs).
- \(t_4\) cannot equal \(t_5,t_6\): forbidden pairs \((4,5),(4,6)\) (2 pairs).

Total pairs among 6 positions: \(\binom{6}{2}=15\).  
Forbidden pairs: \(6\).  
Allowed pairs for the *unique* repeat: \(15-6=9\).

Fix any allowed repeated pair. Then we must assign \(5\) distinct faces to the \(5\) equivalence classes (the repeated pair counts as one class). The number of injective assignments is
\[
(6)_5 = 6\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2 = 720,
\]
and these automatically satisfy the needed inequalities in \(E\) because forbidden equalities are avoided by choosing an allowed pair and making all classes distinct.

Hence
\[
|B\cap E| = 9\cdot 720 = 6480.
\]

### 4) Conditional probability
\[
p = \Pr(B\mid E)=\frac{|B\cap E|}{|E|}=\frac{6480}{14400}=\frac{9}{20}.
\]
So \(m=9,\ n=20\), and \(m+n=29\).

Since \(\pi^6=\mathrm{id}\), we have \(\pi^5\circ \pi=\mathrm{id}\), so \(\pi\) has a left inverse. On a finite set, that implies \(\pi\) is injective, hence bijective, hence a permutation (and automatically onto).

So we are counting permutations in \(S_6\) whose order divides \(6\).

### 2) Cycle structure restriction
A permutation has order equal to the lcm of its cycle lengths. For the order to divide \(6\), every cycle length must divide \(6\). Thus allowed cycle lengths are
\[
1,\;2,\;3,\;6.
\]
So the possible cycle-type partitions of \(6\) using only \(\{1,2,3,6\}\) are:
\[
1^6,\quad 2\,1^4,\quad 2^2 1^2,\quad 2^3,\quad 3\,1^3,\quad 3\,2\,1,\quad 3^2,\quad 6.
\]

### 3) Count each cycle type
For cycle type with \(m_i\) cycles of length \(i\), the number of permutations is
\[
\frac{6!}{\prod_i i^{m_i} m_i!}.
\]

Compute each:

- \(1^6:\ \dfrac{6!}{1^6\cdot 6!}=1\)
- \(2\,1^4:\ \dfrac{6!}{2^1\cdot 1!\cdot 1^4\cdot 4!}=15\)
- \(2^2 1^2:\ \dfrac{6!}{2^2\cdot 2!\cdot 1^2\cdot 2!}=45\)
- \(2^3:\ \dfrac{6!}{2^3\cdot 3!}=15\)
- \(3\,1^3:\ \dfrac{6!}{3^1\cdot 1!\cdot 1^3\cdot 3!}=40\)
- \(3\,2\,1:\ \dfrac{6!}{3^1\cdot 1!\cdot 2^1\cdot 1!\cdot 1^1\cdot 1!}=120\)
- \(3^2:\ \dfrac{6!}{3^2\cdot 2!}=40\)
- \(6:\ \dfrac{6!}{6^1\cdot 1!}=120\)

Sum:
\[
1+15+45+15+40+120+40+120 = 396.
\]

Group the die outcomes into three equally likely categories:

- Alice gets a coin on \(1,2\)  \(\Rightarrow A\) with probability \(1/3\)
- Bob gets a coin on \(3,4\)  \(\Rightarrow B\) with probability \(1/3\)
- Carol gets a coin on \(5,6\) \(\Rightarrow C\) with probability \(1/3\)

We want: Alice and Bob each have at least 2 coins **before Carol gets any**, i.e. before the **first** \(C\) occurs.

---

### 1) Condition on how many non-\(C\) rolls happen before the first \(C\)

Let \(N\) be the number of rolls that are \(A\) or \(B\) before the first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(N=k)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right), \quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]
Given \(N=k\), the first \(k\) outcomes are only \(A\) or \(B\), and by symmetry
\[
\Pr(A)=\Pr(B)=\frac12 \quad \text{(given not \(C\))}
\]
So the number of \(A\)'s among those \(k\) outcomes is \(\text{Binomial}(k,1/2)\).

We need at least 2 \(A\)'s and at least 2 \(B\)'s, i.e.
\[
2 \le \#A \le k-2
\]
This is possible only for \(k\ge 4\).

---

### 2) Compute \(\Pr(2\le \#A \le k-2)\) for \(k\ge 4\)

Exclude the bad cases: \(\#A\in\{0,1,k-1,k\}\).

For \(\#A\sim \text{Bin}(k,1/2)\),
\[
\Pr(\#A=0)=\Pr(\#A=k)=\frac{1}{2^k},\qquad
\Pr(\#A=1)=\Pr(\#A=k-1)=\frac{k}{2^k}
\]
So for \(k\ge 4\),
\[
q_k=\Pr(2\le \#A \le k-2)=1-\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}
\]

---

### 3) Sum over all \(k\ge 4\)

\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \Pr(N=k)\,q_k
=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}\right)
\]
Split into two sums:
\[
P=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k \;-\;\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}
\]
Note \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{1}{2^k}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^k\). Thus:
\[
P=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k \;-\;\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty 2(1+k)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^k
\]

First sum:
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k=\frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}=\frac{16/81}{1/3}=\frac{16}{27}
\]
So it contributes \(\frac13\cdot \frac{16}{27}=\frac{16}{81}\).

Second sum: let \(r=\frac13\). Compute
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty (1+k)r^k
\]
We know
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty r^k=\frac{1}{1-r}=\frac32,\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^\infty kr^k=\frac{r}{(1-r)^2}=\frac34
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (1+k)r^k=\frac32+\frac34=\frac94
\]
Subtract \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
(1+0)r^0=1,\quad (1+1)r^1=\frac23,\quad (1+2)r^2=\frac13,\quad (1+3)r^3=\frac{4}{27}
\]
Sum \(=1+\frac23+\frac13+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}\).

Thus
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty (1+k)r^k=\frac94-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{11}{108}
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty 2(1+k)\left(\frac13\right)^k = 2\cdot \frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{54}
\]
and multiplying by \(\frac13\) gives contribution \(\frac{11}{162}\).

So
\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}
\]

Thus \(m=7,\ n=54\), and
\[
100m+n=700+54=754.
\]

\[
\boxed{754}
\]

Let each roll be classified as:

- \(A\) (Alice gets coin) if 1–2,
- \(B\) (Bob gets coin) if 3–4,
- \(C\) (Carol gets coin) if 5–6.

Each occurs with probability \(1/3\). We roll until the first \(C\) appears; we want Alice and Bob to have **at least 2 coins each** before that happens.

---

### 1) Condition on the number of non-\(C\) rolls
Let \(N\) be the number of rolls before the first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(N=k)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right), \quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]
Given \(N=k\), all \(k\) rolls are \(A\) or \(B\), and conditioned on “not \(C\)”, they are equally likely:
\[
\Pr(A\mid \text{not }C)=\Pr(B\mid \text{not }C)=\frac12.
\]
So given \(N=k\), the number of \(A\)’s is \(\mathrm{Binomial}(k,\tfrac12)\).

We need at least 2 \(A\)’s and at least 2 \(B\)’s, which requires \(k\ge4\). For \(k\ge4\),
\[
\Pr(\text{at least 2 of each}\mid N=k)
=1-\Pr(A\le1)-\Pr(A\ge k-1).
\]
Now
\[
\Pr(A\le1)=\frac{\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}}{2^k}=\frac{1+k}{2^k},
\]
and by symmetry \(\Pr(A\ge k-1)=\frac{1+k}{2^k}\). Hence
\[
\Pr(\text{good}\mid N=k)=1-\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}=1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]

---

### 2) Sum over \(k\ge4\)
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}\right)
= S_1 - S_2.
\]

**First part**
\[
S_1=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac23\right)^k
=\frac13\cdot \frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}
=\frac13\cdot \frac{16/81}{1/3}
=\frac{16}{81}.
\]

**Second part**
\[
S_2=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]
Note
\[
\left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2^k}{3^k}\cdot \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2}{3^k}.
\]
So
\[
S_2=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty (k+1)\cdot \frac{2}{3^k}
=\frac{2}{3}\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}.
\]
Let \(x=\frac13\). Using \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)x^k=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}\),
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)\left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac{1}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{1}{(2/3)^2}=\frac94.
\]
Subtract \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{9}+\frac{4}{27}=1+\frac23+\frac13+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}=\frac94-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{11}{108}.
\]
So
\[
S_2=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]

Therefore
\[
P=S_1-S_2=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32-11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

So \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and
\[
100m+n=700+54=754.
\]

\[
\boxed{754}

Let each roll be classified as:

- \(A\): Alice gets a coin (die shows 1 or 2), probability \(1/3\)
- \(B\): Bob gets a coin (die shows 3 or 4), probability \(1/3\)
- \(C\): Carol gets a coin (die shows 5 or 6), probability \(1/3\)

We want the probability that **before the first \(C\) occurs**, Alice and Bob have each gotten at least 2 coins.

---

### 1) Condition on the number of non-\(C\) rolls before the first \(C\)

Let \(L\) be the number of rolls that are \(A\) or \(B\) before the first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(L=k) = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right), \quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

Given \(L=k\), the \(k\) outcomes are only \(A\) or \(B\). Conditional on “not \(C\)”, \(A\) and \(B\) are equally likely:
\[
\Pr(A)=\Pr(B)=\frac{1}{2}.
\]

We need at least 2 \(A\)'s and at least 2 \(B\)'s, which is only possible for \(k\ge 4\).

---

### 2) For fixed \(k\), compute \(\Pr(\#A\ge 2 \text{ and } \#B\ge 2)\)

Among all \(2^k\) sequences of \(A/B\), the “bad” ones are those with \(\#A\le 1\) or \(\#B\le 1\).

For \(k\ge 4\), these bad cases do not overlap.

- \(\#A=0\): \(1\) sequence
- \(\#A=1\): \(\binom{k}{1}=k\) sequences  
So \(\#A\le 1\) gives \(k+1\) sequences.

Similarly \(\#B\le 1\) gives another \(k+1\) sequences.

Thus good sequences:
\[
2^k - 2(k+1).
\]
So
\[
\Pr(\text{good}\mid L=k)=\frac{2^k-2(k+1)}{2^k}=1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]

---

### 3) Sum over \(k\ge 4\)

\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \Pr(L=k)\Pr(\text{good}\mid L=k)
=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}\right).
\]

Split into two sums:
\[
P=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k \;-\; \frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]

Note:
\[
\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2^k}{3^k}\cdot\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2}{3^k}.
\]
So the second term becomes
\[
\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=4}^\infty (k+1)\cdot \frac{2}{3^k} = \frac{2}{3}\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}.
\]

Compute the first sum:
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k
=\frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}=\frac{16/81}{1/3}=\frac{16}{27}.
\]
So it contributes \(\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{16}{27}=\frac{16}{81}\).

Now compute \(S=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}\). Let \(r=\frac{1}{3}\). Then
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)r^k = \frac{1}{(1-r)^2}.
\]
So for \(r=1/3\),
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}=\frac{1}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{1}{(2/3)^2}=\frac{9}{4}.
\]
Subtract terms \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{9}+\frac{4}{27}
=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{27}
=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
Hence
\[
S=\frac{9}{4}-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{11}{108}.
\]
So the second contribution is
\[
\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]

Therefore
\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

So \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and
\[
100m+n = 700+54=754.
\]

\boxed{754}

So each roll is an independent outcome in \(\{A,B,C\}\) with equal probabilities \(1/3\).

We want the probability that **before the first \(C\)** occurs, both \(A\) and \(B\) have occurred at least twice.

---

### 1) Condition on the number of non-\(C\) outcomes
Let \(N\) be the number of rolls before the first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(N=k)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right),\quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]
because the first \(k\) rolls are not \(C\) (probability \(2/3\) each) and then we get \(C\).

Given \(N=k\), the first \(k\) outcomes are only \(A\) or \(B\), and by symmetry:
\[
\Pr(A)=\Pr(B)=\frac{1/3}{2/3}=\frac12.
\]

We need at least two \(A\)'s and at least two \(B\)'s, which requires \(k\ge 4\), and
\[

\[
p_k=\Pr(2\le \#A \le k-2)=1-\Pr(\#A\le 1)-\Pr(\#A\ge k-1).
\]

\[
\Pr(\#A\le 1)=\frac{\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}}{2^k}=\frac{1+k}{2^k}.
\]
Hence
\[
p_k = 1 - 2\cdot \frac{1+k}{2^k} = 1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]

---

\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \Pr(N=k)\,p_k
=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}\right).

\]

\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k=\frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}=\frac{16/81}{1/3}=\frac{16}{27},
\]
so this contributes \(\frac13\cdot \frac{16}{27}=\frac{16}{81}\).

**Second sum:** simplify the term:
\[
\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2^k}{3^k}\cdot \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2}{3^k}.
\]

\[

= \sum_{k=4}^\infty (k+1)\frac{2}{3^k}
=2\sum_{k=4}^\infty (k+1)\left(\frac13\right)^k.

\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)x^k=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}.
\]

\[

\]
Subtract \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty (k+1)\left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac94-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{11}{108}.
\]

\[
\frac13\cdot \frac{11}{54}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]

\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

Thus \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and

Each roll gives exactly one coin to one of the three players:

- Alice (A) with probability \(2/6=1/3\),
- Bob (B) with probability \(1/3\),
- Carol (C) with probability \(1/3\).

We want
\[
\Pr(\text{Alice and Bob each get }\ge 2\text{ coins before Carol gets any}).
\]
That means: **before the first \(C\) occurs**, the counts of \(A\) and \(B\) must both be at least 2.

---

### 1) Condition on how many non-Carol rolls occur before the first Carol roll
Let \(N\) be the number of rolls **before** the first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(N=n) = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n\left(\frac{1}{3}\right),\quad n\ge 0
\]
because we need \(n\) consecutive non-\(C\) results (probability \(2/3\) each), then a \(C\) (probability \(1/3\)).

Given \(N=n\), each of those \(n\) non-\(C\) rolls is either \(A\) or \(B\), and conditional on “not \(C\)”, we have
\[
\Pr(A)=\Pr(B)=\frac{1/3}{2/3}=\frac12.
\]
So given \(N=n\), the number of Alice coins \(X\) among those \(n\) rolls satisfies
\[
X\sim \text{Binomial}\left(n,\frac12\right),
\]
and Bob’s count is \(n-X\).

We need \(X\ge 2\) and \(n-X\ge 2\), i.e.
\[
2 \le X \le n-2.
\]
This forces \(n\ge 4\).

Thus the desired probability is
\[
\sum_{n=4}^\infty \Pr(N=n)\Pr(2\le X\le n-2\mid N=n).
\]

---

### 2) Compute \(\Pr(2\le X\le n-2)\)
For \(X\sim \text{Bin}(n,1/2)\),
\[
\Pr(2\le X\le n-2)=1-\Pr(X\le 1)-\Pr(X\ge n-1).
\]
By symmetry, \(\Pr(X\le 1)=\Pr(X\ge n-1)\). Also
\[
\Pr(X\le 1)=\frac{\binom n0+\binom n1}{2^n}=\frac{1+n}{2^n}.
\]
So for \(n\ge 4\),
\[
\Pr(2\le X\le n-2)=1-2\cdot\frac{n+1}{2^n}=1-\frac{n+1}{2^{n-1}}.
\]

---

### 3) Sum over \(n\ge 4\)
\[
P=\sum_{n=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{n+1}{2^{n-1}}\right).
\]
Split into two sums:
\[
P=\frac13\sum_{n=4}^\infty\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n \;-\;\frac13\sum_{n=4}^\infty\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n\frac{n+1}{2^{n-1}}.
\]

**First sum:**
\[
\sum_{n=4}^\infty\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n=\frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}=\frac{16/81}{1/3}=\frac{16}{27}.
\]
So it contributes \(\frac13\cdot\frac{16}{27}=\frac{16}{81}\).

**Second sum:** note
\[
\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}=\frac{2^n}{3^n}\cdot\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}=\frac{2}{3^n}.
\]
So the second sum becomes
\[
\frac13\sum_{n=4}^\infty (n+1)\cdot \frac{2}{3^n}=\frac{2}{3}\sum_{n=4}^\infty \frac{n+1}{3^n}.
\]
Let \(r=\frac13\). A known series is
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty (n+1)r^n=\frac{1}{(1-r)^2}.
\]
With \(r=\frac13\),
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{n+1}{3^n}=\frac{1}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{1}{(2/3)^2}=\frac94.
\]
Subtract \(n=0,1,2,3\):
\[
1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{9}+\frac{4}{27}=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{n=4}^\infty \frac{n+1}{3^n}=\frac94-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{243}{108}-\frac{232}{108}=\frac{11}{108}.
\]
So the second term is
\[
\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]

Therefore
\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

Thus \(\frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{54}\), so \(100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754\).

\boxed{754}

Model each die roll only by *who* gets a coin:

- \(A\) (Alice) if 1 or 2, probability \(1/3\)
- \(B\) (Bob) if 3 or 4, probability \(1/3\)
- \(C\) (Carol) if 5 or 6, probability \(1/3\)

We want the probability that we reach “Alice has \(\ge 2\) coins and Bob has \(\ge 2\) coins” **before** the first time \(C\) occurs.

### Markov state setup
Let \(p_{i,j}\) be the probability of eventual success starting from the state where Alice has \(i\) coins and Bob has \(j\) coins, with counts capped at 2 (so \(i,j\in\{0,1,2\}\), where 2 means “at least 2”).

Success state: \(p_{2,2}=1\).

For any other state, on the next roll:
- with probability \(1/3\) we get \(C\) and immediately fail (probability 0),
- with probability \(1/3\) we get \(A\) and move to \((\min(i+1,2), j)\),
- with probability \(1/3\) we get \(B\) and move to \((i, \min(j+1,2))\).

So for \((i,j)\neq(2,2)\),
\[
p_{i,j}=\frac{1}{3}p_{\min(i+1,2),j}+\frac{1}{3}p_{i,\min(j+1,2)}.
\]

### Compute the needed probabilities
1. **State \((2,1)\):**
\[
p_{2,1}=\frac{1}{3}p_{2,1}+\frac{1}{3}p_{2,2}
=\frac{1}{3}p_{2,1}+\frac{1}{3}.
\]
Thus \(\frac{2}{3}p_{2,1}=\frac{1}{3}\Rightarrow p_{2,1}=\frac12.\)

By symmetry, \(p_{1,2}=\frac12\).

2. **State \((2,0)\):**
\[
p_{2,0}=\frac{1}{3}p_{2,0}+\frac{1}{3}p_{2,1}
=\frac{1}{3}p_{2,0}+\frac{1}{6}.
\]
Thus \(\frac{2}{3}p_{2,0}=\frac{1}{6}\Rightarrow p_{2,0}=\frac14.\)

By symmetry, \(p_{0,2}=\frac14\).

3. **State \((1,1)\):**
\[
p_{1,1}=\frac{1}{3}p_{2,1}+\frac{1}{3}p_{1,2}
=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac12+\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac12=\frac13.
\]

4. **State \((1,0)\):**
\[
p_{1,0}=\frac{1}{3}p_{2,0}+\frac{1}{3}p_{1,1}
=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac14+\frac13\right)
=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{7}{12}=\frac{7}{36}.
\]
By symmetry, \(p_{0,1}=\frac{7}{36}\).

5. **Start state \((0,0)\):**
\[
p_{0,0}=\frac{1}{3}p_{1,0}+\frac{1}{3}p_{0,1}
=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{7}{36}+\frac{7}{36}\right)
=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{7}{18}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

So the probability is \(\frac{7}{54}\), already reduced. Hence \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and
\[
100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754.
\]

\[
\boxed{754}
\]

Each roll results in one of three equally likely outcomes:

- Alice gets a coin (die is 1 or 2): probability \(1/3\)
- Bob gets a coin (die is 3 or 4): probability \(1/3\)
- Carol gets a coin (die is 5 or 6): probability \(1/3\)

We roll until the **first** time Carol gets a coin (the first \(C\)). We want the probability that **before this first \(C\)**, both Alice and Bob have received at least 2 coins.

---

### 1) Probability of a fixed \((a,b)\) before the first \(C\)

Suppose before the first Carol coin, Alice gets \(a\) coins and Bob gets \(b\) coins. Then there are \(a+b\) rolls consisting only of \(A\) and \(B\), followed by a \(C\).

- Number of sequences of \(a\) A’s and \(b\) B’s: \(\binom{a+b}{a}\)
- Probability of any particular such sequence followed by \(C\): \((1/3)^{a+b+1}\)

So
\[
\Pr(N_A=a, N_B=b)=\binom{a+b}{a}\left(\frac13\right)^{a+b+1}.
\]

We want \(a\ge2\) and \(b\ge2\).

---

### 2) Sum over total \(k=a+b\)

Let \(k=a+b\). Then \(k\ge4\), and for each \(k\), \(a\) can range from \(2\) to \(k-2\). Thus
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac13\right)^{k+1}\sum_{a=2}^{k-2}\binom{k}{a}.
\]

The inner sum is
\[
\sum_{a=2}^{k-2}\binom{k}{a}
=2^k-\left[\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}+\binom{k}{k-1}+\binom{k}{k}\right]
=2^k-(1+k+k+1)=2^k-2(k+1).
\]

So
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac13\right)^{k+1}\left(2^k-2(k+1)\right).
\]

Split into two sums:
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{2^k}{3^{k+1}}-\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{2(k+1)}{3^{k+1}}.
\]

---

### 3) Compute the sums

First sum:
\[
\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{2^k}{3^{k+1}}
=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^k
=\frac13\cdot \frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}
=\frac13\cdot \frac{16/81}{1/3}
=\frac{16}{81}.
\]

Second sum: let \(j=k+1\), so \(j\ge5\):
\[
\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{2(k+1)}{3^{k+1}}
=2\sum_{j=5}^{\infty}\frac{j}{3^j}.
\]
Use \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty jx^j=\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}\) with \(x=1/3\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{j}{3^j}=\frac{1/3}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{1/3}{(2/3)^2}=\frac34.
\]
Subtract first four terms:
\[
\sum_{j=1}^4 \frac{j}{3^j}=\frac13+\frac{2}{9}+\frac{3}{27}+\frac{4}{81}
=\frac{58}{81}.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{j=5}^{\infty}\frac{j}{3^j}=\frac34-\frac{58}{81}=\frac{11}{324},
\]
and thus the second sum is
\[
2\cdot \frac{11}{324}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]

Therefore
\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

So \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and
\[
100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754.
\]

\[
\boxed{754}
\]

On each roll, exactly one person gets a coin:

- Alice with probability \(1/3\) (roll 1 or 2)
- Bob with probability \(1/3\) (roll 3 or 4)
- Carol with probability \(1/3\) (roll 5 or 6)

We want the probability that **before Carol gets any coins** (i.e., before the first time a 5 or 6 appears), **Alice has at least 2 coins and Bob has at least 2 coins**.

---

### 1) Condition on the number of non-Carol rolls before the first Carol roll
Let \(k\) be the number of rolls that go to Alice or Bob before the first Carol roll occurs. Then:

- The first \(k\) rolls are from \(\{A,B\}\), each with probability \(2/3\)
- The \((k+1)\)-th roll is Carol, with probability \(1/3\)

So,
\[
\Pr(\text{exactly }k\text{ A/B rolls then C})=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right).
\]

Given that a roll is A/B, it is equally likely to be Alice or Bob, so conditioned on \(k\),
\[
A \sim \text{Binomial}\left(k,\frac12\right).
\]

We need \(A\ge2\) and \(B\ge2\), i.e. \(2 \le A \le k-2\). This is only possible for \(k\ge4\).

Let
\[
p_k=\Pr(2\le A\le k-2)=1-\Pr(A=0,1,k-1,k).
\]
Since
\[
\Pr(A=0)=\Pr(A=k)=\frac{1}{2^k},\quad \Pr(A=1)=\Pr(A=k-1)=\frac{k}{2^k},
\]
we get
\[
p_k = 1-\frac{2+2k}{2^k} = 1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]

---

### 2) Sum over all \(k\ge4\)
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}\right).
\]

Split into two sums:
\[
P=\underbrace{\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k}_{S_1}
\;-\;
\underbrace{\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}}_{S_2}.
\]

**Compute \(S_1\):**
\[
S_1=\frac13\cdot \frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}
=\frac13\cdot \frac{(2/3)^4}{1/3}
=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4=\frac{16}{81}.
\]

**Compute \(S_2\):** Note
\[
\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2}{3^k},
\]
so
\[
S_2=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty (k+1)\cdot \frac{2}{3^k}
=\frac{2}{3}\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}.
\]
Let \(x=\frac13\). Then
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)x^k=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}.
\]
So at \(x=\frac13\),
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}=\frac{1}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{1}{(2/3)^2}=\frac94.
\]
Subtract \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{9}+\frac{4}{27}
=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{27}
=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}=\frac94-\frac{58}{27}
=\frac{243}{108}-\frac{232}{108}=\frac{11}{108}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_2=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]

So
\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}
=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}
=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

---

### 3) Finish
\[
\frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{54}\quad\Rightarrow\quad 100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754.
\]

\boxed{754}
\]

Let the outcomes be grouped as follows on each roll:

- \(A\): Alice gets a coin (roll 1 or 2), probability \(1/3\)
- \(B\): Bob gets a coin (roll 3 or 4), probability \(1/3\)
- \(C\): Carol gets a coin (roll 5 or 6), probability \(1/3\)

We roll until the first time \(C\) occurs. Let \(N\) be the number of non-\(C\) rolls before that first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(N=k)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right), \quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]
because we need \(k\) consecutive non-\(C\) results (probability \(2/3\) each), then a \(C\) (probability \(1/3\)).

Conditioned on \(N=k\), all \(k\) rolls are in \(\{A,B\}\), and
\[
\Pr(A)=\Pr(B)=\frac{1/3}{2/3}=\frac12.
\]
So given \(N=k\), the number of \(A\)'s is \(\text{Bin}(k,\tfrac12)\), and \(B=k-A\).

We want Alice and Bob each to have at least 2 coins before Carol gets any, i.e. before the first \(C\). This requires \(k\ge 4\) and
\[
2 \le A \le k-2.
\]
Thus, for \(k\ge 4\),
\[
\Pr(\text{good}\mid N=k)=1-\Pr(A\le 1)-\Pr(A\ge k-1).
\]
By symmetry, \(\Pr(A\le1)=\Pr(A\ge k-1)\), and
\[
\Pr(A\le1)=\frac{\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}}{2^k}=\frac{1+k}{2^k}.
\]
So
\[
\Pr(\text{good}\mid N=k)=1-2\cdot\frac{1+k}{2^k}=1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]

Therefore the desired probability is
\[
\Pr(\text{good})=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}\right).
\]
Compute it as
\[
\Pr(\text{good})=\frac13\left[\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k \;-\; \sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}\right].
\]

First sum:
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k=\frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}=\frac{16/81}{1/3}=\frac{16}{27}.
\]

Second sum: note
\[
\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2^k}{3^k}\cdot\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2}{3^k},
\]
so
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}
=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{2(k+1)}{3^k}.
\]
Let \(r=\frac13\). Using \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)r^k=\frac{1}{(1-r)^2}\), we get
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}=\frac{1}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{9}{4}.
\]
Subtract \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{9}+\frac{4}{27}=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^k}=\frac{9}{4}-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{11}{108},
\]
and thus
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{2(k+1)}{3^k}=2\cdot\frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{54}.
\]

Put it together:
\[
\Pr(\text{good})=\frac13\left(\frac{16}{27}-\frac{11}{54}\right)
=\frac13\left(\frac{32-11}{54}\right)
=\frac13\cdot\frac{21}{54}
=\frac{7}{54}.
\]
So \(\frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{54}\), and
\[
100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754.
\]

Group the die outcomes into three equally likely types:

- \(A=\{1,2\}\) gives Alice a coin, probability \(1/3\)
- \(B=\{3,4\}\) gives Bob a coin, probability \(1/3\)
- \(C=\{5,6\}\) gives Carol a coin, probability \(1/3\)

We roll until the first \(C\) occurs. Let \(N\) be the number of rolls before the first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(N=k)=\left(\frac23\right)^k\left(\frac13\right),\quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]
Conditioned on “not \(C\),” each roll is \(A\) or \(B\) with equal probability \(1/2\). So given \(N=k\), the number of \(A\)’s is \(\mathrm{Bin}(k,1/2)\), and we want at least 2 \(A\)’s and at least 2 \(B\)’s. This requires \(k\ge 4\).

For \(k\ge 4\), the bad events “Alice gets 0 or 1 coin” and “Bob gets 0 or 1 coin” are disjoint, so
\[
\Pr(\text{at least 2 each}\mid N=k)
=1-2\Pr(\text{Alice gets}\le1\mid N=k).
\]
Now
\[
\Pr(\text{Alice}\le 1\mid N=k)=\frac{\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}}{2^k}=\frac{1+k}{2^k},
\]
so for \(k\ge 4\),
\[
\Pr(\text{at least 2 each}\mid N=k)=1-\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}.
\]

Thus the desired probability is
\[
\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^k\left(\frac13\right)\left(1-\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}\right).
\]
Split into two sums:
\[
\underbrace{\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac13\right)\left(\frac23\right)^k}_{S_1}
-\underbrace{\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac13\right)\left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}}_{S_2}.
\]

### Compute \(S_1\)
\[
S_1=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^k
=\frac13\cdot \frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}
=\frac13\cdot \frac{16/81}{1/3}
=\frac{16}{81}.
\]

### Compute \(S_2\)
Note \(\left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{1}{2^k}=\left(\frac13\right)^k\). So
\[
S_2=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{2(1+k)}{3^{k+1}}.
\]
Let \(a=\frac13\). Then
\[
\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{2(1+k)}{3^{k+1}}
=2\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}(1+k)a^{k+1}
=2a\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}(1+k)a^k.
\]
We use
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(1+k)a^k=\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{a}{(1-a)^2}.
\]
With \(a=\frac13\), this equals
\[
\frac{1}{2/3}+\frac{1/3}{(2/3)^2}=\frac32+\frac34=\frac94.
\]
Subtract the first four terms \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{3}(1+k)a^k = 1+\frac23+\frac13+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}(1+k)a^k=\frac94-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{11}{108}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_2=2a\cdot \frac{11}{108}=2\cdot \frac13\cdot \frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]

### Final probability
\[
S_1-S_2=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]
Thus \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and
\[
100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754.
\]

Let the outcomes be grouped as:

- \(A\): Alice gets a coin (roll 1 or 2), probability \(1/3\)
- \(B\): Bob gets a coin (roll 3 or 4), probability \(1/3\)
- \(C\): Carol gets a coin (roll 5 or 6), probability \(1/3\)

We roll until the first time \(C\) occurs. We want the probability that **before** that first \(C\), Alice has received at least 2 coins and Bob has received at least 2 coins.

---

### 1) Probability of getting \(i\) A’s and \(j\) B’s before the first C
To have exactly \(i\) A’s and \(j\) B’s before the first \(C\), we need:

- a length \(i+j\) sequence consisting of \(i\) A’s and \(j\) B’s in any order
- followed by a \(C\)

Number of such sequences: \(\binom{i+j}{i}\).

Each specific sequence has probability \((1/3)^{i+j}\), and the final \(C\) has probability \(1/3\), so:
\[
\Pr(i,j)=\binom{i+j}{i}\left(\frac13\right)^{i+j+1}.
\]

We need \(i\ge2\) and \(j\ge2\), so the desired probability is
\[
P=\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\binom{i+j}{i}\left(\frac13\right)^{i+j+1}.
\]
Let \(x=\frac13\). Then
\[
P=x\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\binom{i+j}{i}x^{i+j}.
\]
Define
\[
S=\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\binom{i+j}{i}x^{i+j},
\quad\text{so } P=xS.
\]

---

### 2) Compute \(S\) by subtraction from the full sum
A known generating function identity is:
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\binom{i+j}{i}a^i b^j=\frac{1}{1-a-b}.
\]
Setting \(a=b=x\) gives the full sum
\[
T=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\binom{i+j}{i}x^{i+j}=\frac{1}{1-2x}.
\]

Now subtract cases where \(i<2\) or \(j<2\). Let
\[
A=\sum_{i=0}^{1}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\binom{i+j}{i}x^{i+j}.
\]
Compute \(A\):
- For \(i=0\): \(\sum_{j\ge0} x^j=\frac{1}{1-x}\)
- For \(i=1\): \(\sum_{j\ge0} (j+1)x^{j+1}=x\sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)x^j=\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}\)

So
\[
A=\frac{1}{1-x}+\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}.
\]
By symmetry, the same sum for \(j=0,1\) is also \(A\).

The overlap (both \(i<2\) and \(j<2\)) is
\[
C=\sum_{i=0}^{1}\sum_{j=0}^{1}\binom{i+j}{i}x^{i+j}
=1+2x+2x^2.
\]

Thus by inclusion-exclusion,
\[
S=T-2A+C=\frac{1}{1-2x}-\frac{2}{(1-x)^2}+\left(1+2x+2x^2\right).
\]

---

### 3) Plug in \(x=\frac13\)
\[
\frac{1}{1-2x}=\frac{1}{1-\frac23}=3,
\quad
\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac23\right)^2}=\frac{9}{4},
\quad
1+2x+2x^2=1+\frac23+\frac{2}{9}=\frac{17}{9}.
\]
So
\[
S=3-2\cdot\frac94+\frac{17}{9}
=3-\frac92+\frac{17}{9}
=\frac{7}{18}.
\]
Therefore
\[
P=xS=\frac13\cdot\frac{7}{18}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

So \(\frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{54}\), and
\[
100m+n = 100\cdot 7 + 54 = 754.
\]

- \(A\): Alice gets a coin \((1,2)\) with probability \(1/3\)
- \(B\): Bob gets a coin \((3,4)\) with probability \(1/3\)
- \(C\): Carol gets a coin \((5,6)\) with probability \(1/3\)

We want the probability that **before the first \(C\)** occurs, we have at least 2 \(A\)’s and at least 2 \(B\)’s.

---

### 1) Condition on when the first \(C\) occurs
Suppose the first \(C\) occurs on roll \(k+1\). Then the first \(k\) rolls are only \(A\) or \(B\), and roll \(k+1\) is \(C\).

This forces \(k\ge 4\), because we need at least 2 coins for each of Alice and Bob.

For a fixed \(k\ge4\), the probability is:
\[
\Pr(\text{first }k\text{ are }A/B,\ \#A\ge2,\ \#B\ge2,\ \text{then }C)
= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{k+1}\cdot \#(\text{good }A/B\text{ strings of length }k).
\]

---

### 2) Count good \(A/B\) strings of length \(k\)
There are \(2^k\) total strings of \(A/B\) of length \(k\).

Bad strings are those with fewer than 2 \(A\)’s or fewer than 2 \(B\)’s:

- \(\#A=0\): \(1\) string (all \(B\))
- \(\#A=1\): \(\binom{k}{1}=k\) strings
- \(\#B=0\): \(1\) string (all \(A\))
- \(\#B=1\): \(\binom{k}{1}=k\) strings

So bad total \(=2+2k\). Hence good:
\[
T_k = 2^k-(2k+2)=2^k-2(k+1).
\]

---

### 3) Sum over all \(k\ge4\)
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{k+1}\left(2^k-2(k+1)\right)
= \underbrace{\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{2^k}{3^{k+1}}}_{S_1}
-2\underbrace{\sum_{k=4}^\infty \frac{k+1}{3^{k+1}}}_{S_2}.
\]

#### Compute \(S_1\)
\[
S_1=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k
=\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}
=\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{16/81}{1/3}
=\frac{16}{81}.
\]

#### Compute \(S_2\)
Let \(j=k+1\), so \(j=5,6,7,\dots\):
\[
S_2=\sum_{j=5}^\infty \frac{j}{3^j}.
\]
Use the known series \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty jx^j=\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}\). With \(x=\frac13\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{j}{3^j}=\frac{1/3}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{1/3}{(2/3)^2}=\frac{3}{4}.
\]
Subtract the first four terms:
\[
\sum_{j=1}^4 \frac{j}{3^j}=\frac13+\frac{2}{9}+\frac{3}{27}+\frac{4}{81}
=\frac{58}{81}.
\]
So
\[
S_2=\frac{3}{4}-\frac{58}{81}=\frac{11}{324}.
\]

---

### 4) Final probability
\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-2\cdot\frac{11}{324}
=\frac{64}{324}-\frac{22}{324}
=\frac{42}{324}
=\frac{7}{54}.
\]
Thus \(\frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{54}\), so \(100m+n=700+54=754\).

\[
\boxed{754}
\]

Each roll has three equally likely “coin recipients”:

- Alice (1 or 2): probability \(1/3\)
- Bob (3 or 4): probability \(1/3\)
- Carol (5 or 6): probability \(1/3\)

We want the probability that **before the first time Carol gets a coin**, Alice and Bob have **each** gotten at least 2 coins.

---

### 1) Condition on how many non-Carol rolls occur before the first Carol roll
Let \(L\) be the number of rolls **before** the first Carol roll. Then \(L\) has a geometric distribution with “success” = Carol:

\[
\Pr(L=k)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right),\quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

Given \(L=k\), all \(k\) rolls are either Alice or Bob, equally likely, so the number of Alice coins \(A\) is

\[
A\mid (L=k)\sim \text{Binomial}\left(k,\frac{1}{2}\right)
\]

Bob then has \(k-A\) coins.

We need \(A\ge 2\) and \(k-A\ge 2\), i.e.
\[
2\le A\le k-2
\]
This requires \(k\ge 4\).

---

### 2) Probability of getting at least 2 for each, given \(L=k\)
For \(k\ge 4\),
\[
\Pr(2\le A\le k-2)=1-\Pr(A\le 1)-\Pr(A\ge k-1)
\]
By symmetry of the binomial with \(p=1/2\),
\[
\Pr(A\le 1)=\frac{\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}}{2^k}=\frac{1+k}{2^k}
\]
and \(\Pr(A\ge k-1)=\frac{1+k}{2^k}\). Thus
\[
\Pr(2\le A\le k-2)=1-\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}
\]

---

### 3) Sum over all \(k\ge 4\)
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{2(1+k)}{2^k}\right)
\]
Factor \(\frac{1}{3}\):
\[
P=\frac{1}{3}\left[\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k \;-\; 2\sum_{k=4}^\infty (1+k)\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{1}{2^k}\right]
\]
Note \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\frac{1}{2^k}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^k\). So
\[
P=\frac{1}{3}\left[\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k \;-\; 2\sum_{k=4}^\infty (1+k)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^k\right]
\]

Compute the geometric sum:
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k=\frac{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4}{1-\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{\frac{16}{81}}{\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{16}{27}
\]

Let \(r=\frac{1}{3}\). For
\[
S=\sum_{k=4}^\infty (1+k)r^k
\]
First compute from \(k=0\) to \(\infty\):
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty r^k=\frac{1}{1-r}=\frac{3}{2},\quad \sum_{k=0}^\infty k r^k=\frac{r}{(1-r)^2}=\frac{3}{4}
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (1+k)r^k=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{4}=\frac{9}{4}
\]
Subtract \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
(1+k)r^k = 1,\ \frac{2}{3},\ \frac{1}{3},\ \frac{4}{27}
\]
Sum \(=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}\).

Thus
\[
S=\frac{9}{4}-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{243-232}{108}=\frac{11}{108}
\]

Now plug back:
\[
P=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{16}{27}-2\cdot \frac{11}{108}\right]
=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{16}{27}-\frac{11}{54}\right]
=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{32-11}{54}\right]
=\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{21}{54}
=\frac{7}{54}
\]

So \(\frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{54}\), hence \(100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754\).

\[
\boxed{754}

Each roll gives a coin to exactly one person, with probabilities  
\[
P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=\frac{2}{6}=\frac13.
\]

We want the probability that **before Carol gets any coins**, Alice has at least 2 coins and Bob has at least 2 coins.

---

### 1) Condition on the number of non-Carol rolls before the first Carol roll
Let \(K\) be the number of rolls that are **not** \(C\) (i.e., are \(A\) or \(B\)) before the first \(C\) occurs.

Since each roll is \(C\) with probability \(1/3\), we have a geometric distribution (counting failures before the first success):
\[
P(K=k)=\left(\frac23\right)^k\left(\frac13\right), \quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

Given that a roll is not \(C\), it is equally likely to be \(A\) or \(B\), so conditional on \(K=k\), the \(k\) rolls are i.i.d. with
\[
P(A)=P(B)=\frac12.
\]

---

### 2) For a fixed \(k\), compute the chance Alice and Bob each have at least 2 coins
If \(K=k\), then Alice’s coin count \(X\sim \text{Binomial}(k,1/2)\), and Bob has \(k-X\).

We need:
\[
X\ge 2 \quad \text{and}\quad k-X\ge 2 \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; 2\le X\le k-2.
\]
This is only possible when \(k\ge 4\).

So for \(k\ge 4\),
\[
P(2\le X\le k-2)=1-P(X=0,1,k-1,k).
\]
Compute the bad cases:
\[
P(X=0)=\frac{1}{2^k},\quad P(X=1)=\frac{k}{2^k},\quad P(X=k-1)=\frac{k}{2^k},\quad P(X=k)=\frac{1}{2^k}.
\]
Thus
\[
P(2\le X\le k-2)=1-\frac{2+2k}{2^k}=1-\frac{2(k+1)}{2^k}.
\]

---

### 3) Sum over all \(k\ge 4\)
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty} P(K=k)\,P(2\le X\le k-2\mid K=k)
=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^k\left(\frac13\right)\left(1-\frac{2(k+1)}{2^k}\right).
\]
Split into two sums:
\[
P=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^k-\frac13\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{2(k+1)}{2^k}.
\]

First sum:
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac23\right)^k=\frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}=\frac{16/81}{1/3}=\frac{16}{27}.
\]

Second sum: note \(\left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{1}{2^k}=\left(\frac13\right)^k\), so
\[
\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{2(k+1)}{2^k}
=2\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{k+1}{3^k}.
\]
Let \(r=\frac13\). Use \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)r^k=\frac{1}{(1-r)^2}\):
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)\left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac{1}{(1-1/3)^2}=\frac{1}{(2/3)^2}=\frac94.
\]
Subtract \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
\sum_{k=0}^3 (k+1)\left(\frac13\right)^k
=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{9}+\frac{4}{27}
=1+\frac23+\frac13+\frac{4}{27}=2+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{58}{27}.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=4}^\infty (k+1)\left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac94-\frac{58}{27}=\frac{11}{108}.
\]
Hence the second sum is
\[
2\cdot \frac{11}{108}=\frac{11}{54}.
\]

Putting it together:
\[
P=\frac13\left(\frac{16}{27}-\frac{11}{54}\right)
=\frac13\left(\frac{32}{54}-\frac{11}{54}\right)
=\frac13\cdot \frac{21}{54}
=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

So \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and
\[
100m+n=700+54=754.
\]

\[
\boxed{754}
\]

Let each roll award a coin to:

- Alice (A) with probability \( \frac13\) (die shows 1 or 2),
- Bob (B) with probability \( \frac13\) (die shows 3 or 4),
- Carol (C) with probability \( \frac13\) (die shows 5 or 6).

We need the probability that **before the first time Carol gets any coin**, Alice and Bob have **each** gotten at least 2 coins.  
Equivalently: looking at the sequence of rolls **before the first \(C\)** appears, the counts of \(A\) and \(B\) are both \(\ge 2\).

---

### 1) Condition on the number of non-\(C\) rolls before the first \(C\)

Let \(N\) be the number of rolls that are not \(C\) before the first \(C\). Then
\[
\Pr(N=k) = \left(\frac23\right)^k\left(\frac13\right), \quad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]
Given \(N=k\), each of those \(k\) rolls is either \(A\) or \(B\), and conditional probabilities are
\[
\Pr(A \mid \text{not } C)=\Pr(B \mid \text{not } C)=\frac12.
\]

For fixed \(k\), we need at least 2 A’s and at least 2 B’s among \(k\) fair coin flips, i.e. if \(a\) is the number of A’s then
\[
2 \le a \le k-2.
\]
Thus for \(k\ge 4\),
\[
P_k=\Pr(\text{at least 2 A and 2 B} \mid N=k)=\frac{1}{2^k}\sum_{a=2}^{k-2}\binom{k}{a}.
\]
The excluded cases are \(a=0,1,k-1,k\), so
\[
\sum_{a=2}^{k-2}\binom{k}{a}=2^k-\left[\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}+\binom{k}{k-1}+\binom{k}{k}\right]
=2^k-(1+k+k+1)=2^k-2k-2.
\]
So
\[
P_k=\frac{2^k-2k-2}{2^k}=1-\frac{2k+2}{2^k}.
\]

---

### 2) Compute the total probability

\[
\Pr(\text{desired})=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \Pr(N=k)\,P_k
=\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac23\right)^k\left(\frac13\right)\cdot \frac{2^k-2k-2}{2^k}.
\]
Note \(\left(\frac23\right)^k\frac{1}{2^k}=\left(\frac13\right)^k\), so:
\[
\Pr(\text{desired})=\frac13\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac13\right)^k(2^k-2k-2).
\]
Split into three sums:
\[
\Pr(\text{desired})=\frac13\left[\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac23\right)^k
-2\sum_{k=4}^\infty k\left(\frac13\right)^k
-2\sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac13\right)^k\right].
\]

Compute each:

1. \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac23\right)^k=\frac{(2/3)^4}{1-2/3}=\frac{16/81}{1/3}=\frac{16}{27}.\)

2. Use \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^\infty kr^k=\frac{r}{(1-r)^2}\) with \(r=\frac13\):
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty k\left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac{1/3}{(2/3)^2}=\frac{3}{4}.
\]
Subtract first terms \(k=0,1,2,3\):
\[
1\cdot\frac13+2\cdot\frac19+3\cdot\frac1{27}=\frac13+\frac29+\frac19=\frac23.
\]
So \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=4}^\infty k\left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac34-\frac23=\frac1{12}.\)

3. \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=4}^\infty \left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac{(1/3)^4}{1-1/3}=\frac{1/81}{2/3}=\frac1{54}.\)

Now plug in:
\[
\Pr(\text{desired})=\frac13\left[\frac{16}{27}-2\cdot\frac1{12}-2\cdot\frac1{54}\right]
=\frac13\left[\frac{16}{27}-\frac16-\frac1{27}\right]
=\frac13\left[\frac{15}{27}-\frac16\right]
=\frac13\left[\frac59-\frac16\right]
=\frac13\cdot\frac{7}{18}
=\frac{7}{54}.
\]

So \(\frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{54}\) with \((m,n)=1\). Then
\[
100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754.
\]

\boxed{754}

Each roll results in one of three outcomes with equal probability \(1/3\):

- \(A\): Alice gets a coin (die \(1,2\))
- \(B\): Bob gets a coin (die \(3,4\))
- \(C\): Carol gets a coin (die \(5,6\))

We want the probability that **before the first \(C\)** occurs, Alice has at least 2 coins and Bob has at least 2 coins.

Let the number of rolls before the first \(C\) be \(k\). Then:

- The probability that the first \(k\) rolls are in \(\{A,B\}\) and the \((k+1)\)-st roll is \(C\) is  
  \[
  \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right).
  \]
- Given that the first \(k\) rolls are only \(A\) or \(B\), they are equally likely, so the number of \(A\)'s in those \(k\) rolls is \(\text{Binomial}(k,1/2)\).

We need at least 2 of each, i.e. the number of \(A\)'s is between \(2\) and \(k-2\). The “bad” cases are:
- \(A=0,1\) or \(A=k,k-1\).

So for \(k\ge 4\),
\[
P(\text{good}\mid k)=1-\frac{\binom{k}{0}+\binom{k}{1}+\binom{k}{k-1}+\binom{k}{k}}{2^k}
=1-\frac{1+k+k+1}{2^k}
=1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}.
\]

Therefore the desired probability is
\[
P=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(1-\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}\right)
=S_1-S_2,
\]
where
\[
S_1=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=\frac{16}{81},
\]
and
\[
S_2=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\frac{k+1}{2^{k-1}}
=\sum_{k=4}^{\infty}\frac{2(k+1)}{3^{k+1}}.
\]
Let \(j=k+1\), so \(j\ge 5\):
\[
S_2=\sum_{j=5}^{\infty}\frac{2j}{3^j}
=2\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{j}{3^j}-\sum_{j=1}^{4}\frac{j}{3^j}\right).
\]
Using \(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} j r^j = \frac{r}{(1-r)^2}\) with \(r=\frac13\),
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{j}{3^j}=\frac{1/3}{(2/3)^2}=\frac34.
\]
And
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{4}\frac{j}{3^j}=\frac13+\frac{2}{9}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{4}{81}=\frac{58}{81}.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{j=5}^{\infty}\frac{j}{3^j}=\frac34-\frac{58}{81}=\frac{11}{324},
\quad
S_2=2\cdot \frac{11}{324}=\frac{11}{162}.
\]
Thus
\[
P=\frac{16}{81}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{32}{162}-\frac{11}{162}=\frac{21}{162}=\frac{7}{54}.
\]
So \(m=7\), \(n=54\), and
\[
100m+n=100\cdot 7+54=754.
\]

\boxed{754}

---

Let \(N\) be the number of rolls that are **not** Carol (i.e., are Alice or Bob) before the first Carol roll. Then \(N\) has a geometric distribution:

\[

\]

\[

and Bob’s count is \(B=k-A\). We need \(A\ge2\) and \(B\ge2\), i.e.

\[

\]

---

### 2) Compute \(\Pr(2 \le A \le k-2 \mid N=k)\)

For \(A\sim \text{Binomial}(k,1/2)\),

\[

\]

By symmetry, \(\Pr(A\ge k-1)=\Pr(A\le1)=\frac{k+1}{2^k}\). Thus

\[
\Pr(2\le A\le k-2)=1-2\cdot \frac{k+1}{2^k}
\]

---

\[

\[

So
\[

Hence
\[

\[
